cia-0000119581:
A November 1964 CIA special report describes Czechoslovakia trying a new role inside the Soviet bloc. Prague was testing how much room Moscow would grant a loyal ally. That question would return with far higher stakes four years later.

The report follows the early stages of that experiment. Small shifts in a satellite state's foreign and economic policy mattered to Washington because they hinted at looseness in Soviet control. For readers, the paper shows the long buildup to 1968. The Prague Spring did not appear from nowhere. Analysts had been tracking Prague's search for room to move since the mid-1960s.
cia-0000126881: A September 1968 CIA report covers the treatment of Czechoslovak leaders during their forced stay in Moscow. Dubcek and his colleagues had been summoned to the Kremlin and pressed into submission after the invasion. The paper documents that strong-arming as the agency learned of it. The Moscow meetings ended with the Czechoslovak leaders signing terms they had crossed a border hoping to refuse, the hinge on which the Prague Spring closed.
cia-0000132481: A widening rift between Venezuela and Cuba is forecast in item 6 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated April 5, 1960. Caracas and Havana were drifting apart month by month. Within two years Venezuela would break relations with Cuba entirely. The short item records the state of the quarrel that spring, well before the final break made headlines across the hemisphere.
cia-0000132581: Brazil's president-elect possibly trying to mediate fills item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the word between, leaving the parties unnamed. Brazil's incoming leader was placing himself as a peacemaker in the hemisphere's quarrels. The short item reports the possible mediation effort.
cia-0000135881: Routing sheet in the declassified files, dated 2 January 1954, covers briefing notes tied to the name Calibaris, routed through the office with a memo attached. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136081: Dated 3 March 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records closing down SARANAC, ending a coded project whose work was done, or whose cover was blown. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136381: Castillo must be contacted, Washington agrees in this March 1952 cable, two years before he led the Guatemala invasion. The contact should learn the opposing forces, the opportunity for buying support among the army, Guardia Civil, and key officials, and how unbuyable forces might be immobilized through student or labor action. All details needed to estimate the proposed movement's success are requested, with a full report to follow. Signed by J. C. King, it is an early seed of PBSUCCESS.
cia-0000136981: Spares and supplies are moving on the most urgent basis. This late June 1954 status report tells LINCOLN so. Spares for P-51s will arrive 29 and 30 June. Three P-51s will proceed on 28 June. Headquarters is recruiting up to twenty cargo handlers. They will travel on supply flights from 28 June. A supply officer and two technicians are also sought. They will inventory the huge stock of spares. Some spares may later be repacked for onward shipment.
un-ga-res-a-69-81:
A full ban on nuclear tests is pressed toward force in Resolution A/69/81, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The halt of all test blasts, the text holds, is a real step toward disarmament and against the spread of such arms. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was adopted in 1996 and opened for signing that same month. After more than fifteen years, its entry into force is called more urgent than ever.

The counts are laid out with pride. One hundred eighty-three states had signed the pact, among them 41 of the 44 whose assent is needed to bring it to life. One hundred sixty-three had ratified it, three of them nuclear-armed states. The holdouts are named by their absence, not by blame.
un-ga-res-181:
Palestine's fate was set on a new course by Resolution 181, adopted by the General Assembly on 29 November 1947. Britain, which ruled the land under a League mandate, had asked for a UN study of its future rule. A special team toured the land and heard all sides. Its main plan, backed by most of the team, was partition with a shared trade union.

The Assembly urges Britain and all member states to adopt and carry out that plan. Palestine would split into two states, one Jewish and one Arab, linked in trade. Jerusalem would stand apart, under world rule. Britain's pull-out was set for 1 August 1948. The plan lit the war of 1948, and its two-state frame still shapes the debate.
un-sc-res-81: First rules for its own acts were noted by the Security Council in Resolution 81, passed on 24 May 1950. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a note of May 1949 on the point. The Council takes note of an Assembly text of 28 April 1949 on the same ground. It rules that, should a fit chance arise, it will base its acts on the rules held in that text. The vote passed with all in favor, the Soviet member being absent from the hall.
un-sc-res-681: Security Council business produced Resolution 681, catalogued in this library as a 1949 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1381: With a catalog date of 2001, Resolution 1381 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1481: Resolution 1481 dates to 2003, when the Security Council issued it as part of its regular business on peace and security. Wikisource's transcription of the official record is the source of the text kept here. Readers find the Council's standard architecture inside: recitals first, then decisions written to be quoted word for word by diplomats.
un-sc-res-1681: Under number 1681, the fifteen-member Security Council filed a formal decision, preserved here via a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The document's two movements are easy to spot: the Council first tells the world what it sees, then tells it what will be done. The entry preserves both movements in full.
un-sc-res-1881: Security Council Resolution 1881 is held here as a transcription of the United Nations official record from English Wikisource. The Council's authority is collective, and the text is where that collectivity becomes visible: fifteen positions merged into one set of findings and decisions. The merged result is preserved entire in this entry.
cia-0000132681:
Only two days after a March 1 companion, this CIA briefing on Cuba is dated March 3, 1961. The Bay of Pigs landing was about six weeks away. Updates were coming fast enough that a two-day gap merited a fresh paper.

That pace is the story here: by March, Cuba reporting had become a near-daily service for a government closing in on an invasion decision. Each short paper refreshed the last, tracking an island whose defenses and politics decided the plan's odds. The declassified text survives via the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132781:
Election season colors this Cuban Developments entry of September 4, 1960. In the United States, Kennedy and Nixon were campaigning for the presidency, and Cuba had become one of their issues. The CIA's running series kept reporting through the contest.

The paper belongs to the pre-election file both campaigns argued over: how the revolution had happened and what to do about it. Its September date places it two months before voters decided. For readers, the briefing links intelligence reporting to a famous campaign, in which Cuba's fate at home and abroad were debated together.
cia-0000135681: Brigade 2506's Spanish files include this document dated 1 March 1961, the start of the brigade's last full month before the April landing in Cuba. The force of anti-Castro exiles had been built and trained by the CIA over the previous year. The catalog records no subject for this item. It remains a primary source in Spanish, dated and placed within the brigade's papers, and its contents are for the reader of the text to establish.
cia-0000139481: Filed in 1988 under Project SUN STREAK, document 0000139481 comes from the last phase of the government's remote viewing work. Viewers in the program sat with little more than map references and tried to report what stood at the target, while monitors logged each claim. The record does not mark this file as special within the series. Declassified along with the program's other papers, it is part of the fullest public account of official psychic spying.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d81: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt dated October 31, 1943 is Document 81 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister's two notes that day closed out the October correspondence in this series. What divided their business, the record does not say, and a summary should not guess. Both letters are printed in the Foreign Relations volume, at the point where the story turns toward the President's journey east.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d181: The Most Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, stands as Document 181 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, beside its companion Secret Protocol of the same date. The higher stamp marked the more sensitive of the agreed texts, the one fewest eyes were meant to see. That it is printed at all shows how far time opens wartime files. The protocol appears in the Foreign Relations series, at the close of the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d281:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404/1 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, answering the American agenda for the Sextant Conference. Signed by Brooke, Portal, and Cunningham, it raises no objection to the American subjects but proposes a simpler order of business.

Five main heads are listed: reaffirming the overall objective and basic undertakings, Southeast Asia operations, Overlord and the Mediterranean, the war against Japan, and progress reports. Southeast Asia is put second, so Chiang Kai-shek and Mountbatten can join the talks at the earliest stage. Detailed points from the American list would be fitted in from day to day, and progress reports left to the end, once the big items were settled.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d381:
A secret report from the Office of Strategic Services gives an account of a visit to Tito's National Army of Liberation in Yugoslavia. It was written at Bari in Italy on 29 October 1943. Its author spent six weeks in the field with the Partisans, from mid-September to late October.

His conclusions run against outside assumptions. The Partisan movement, he writes, is of far greater weight than the world realizes. By their own efforts, ringed by Germans, Italians, Ustasha, and Chetniks, the Partisans have built a free community. In it, Muslims, Christians, Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and Communists may all speak on how it should be run. The Communist Party failed to organize the movement on party lines and threw every force against the common enemy, though its members work hard to shape the new state's future. Villagers with kin in America greeted the mission with embarrassing faith in American aid.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d481:
On December 5, 1943, in the middle of the Second Cairo Conference, Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy again wrote to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant. McCloy had written to Hopkins the day before as well. The State Department printed this second message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Repeated staff-level messages during a summit usually track problems being worked in real time: questions from the conference floor sent home, answers and material sent back. The McCloy-Hopkins channel was one of the busiest in wartime Washington. Read together, their December messages show the staff machinery that kept the President supplied while he negotiated abroad.
frus-1944-quebec-d81: Under the number 81, the Quebec 1944 volume prints a short editorial note. Its historians added such notes wherever the paper record needed help. A note may supply context, name a figure, or flag another document. The surrounding papers were prepared for the September 1944 conference. At Quebec, the American and British leaders took up Germany's future and the Pacific war. Treat this note as the editors pausing to orient the reader.
frus-1944-quebec-d181:
No participant's official memorandum survives for the dinner meeting of September 13, 1944, so the editors assemble accounts from Leahy's diary, Lord Moran's diary, and later recollections. Shipping was the announced subject, but Moran records that how to prevent another war with Germany was the only subject of conversation all evening. The Americans argued for drastic action against German industry.

Morgenthau wanted the Ruhr closed down, which would help British exports, especially steel. Churchill resisted: "I agree with Burke. You cannot indict a whole nation." He favored disarmament, but insisted Germany be allowed to live decently. Punishment should be swift: "Kill the criminals, but don't carry on the business for years." Cherwell sided with the Americans. Morgenthau later recalled Churchill calling the plan chaining England to a dead body.
frus-1944-quebec-d281:
Roosevelt's message to Chiang Kai-shek of September 16, 1944, is one of the bluntest in the volume. After reading the latest reports from China, he wrote, his chiefs and he were convinced Chiang faced the disaster long feared. The Y Force troops across the Salween had fought with great courage, but unless reinforced and supported with every capacity, their sacrifices would be valueless.

Withdrawal, Roosevelt warned, was exactly what the Japanese were striving to cause. If Chiang failed to man his divisions, the land line to China would never open and the Hump air route would be jeopardized. For that, Chiang must accept the consequences and assume personal responsibility. Stilwell, he noted, still had not been given command of all forces in China.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d81:
Soviet staff kept phoning the American Embassy with questions, Harriman reported on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It shows the Foreign Office staff puzzling over the sense of Roosevelt's plan for voting in the new world body.

A Soviet aide named Bereshkov had called an embassy secretary more than once. He even asked if some error in the wires had crept into the text. His puzzle was one part of the plan, on settling local disputes through groups of nearby states. Harriman says the embassy staff gave their reading of it. He asks Washington at once: must Moscow accept that part now, or can it wait?
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d181:
Italy's cabinet crisis, and a British veto delivered inside it, fill this excerpt from the Secretary of State's briefing of 1 December 1944. The memorandum for the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Ambassador Kirk's reports from Rome supply the news.

Kirk has told Premier Bonomi of Washington's concern over the long crisis. The United States will not judge the make-up of a new Italian government, but it must honor Italy's past pledges to the allies. The British ambassador, by contrast, told Bonomi flatly that Count Sforza as foreign minister would be unacceptable. Kirk calls that undue meddling in Italian home affairs. Winant has been told to voice American regret in London, since the move angered the Italian left and drew sharp comment in the American press.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d281:
Ships for soldiers or ships for hungry civilians? McCloy's excerpt of 23 January 1945 states the armed services' hard answer. His memorandum to the Secretary of State, on the shipping situation and the Law Mission, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Hopkins and Justice Byrnes, both bound for the conference, know the Law Mission's story well. Law stated the need for a civilian rebuilding program for Europe, France and Belgium above all, most forcibly; Monnet followed with another appeal. The danger is real, McCloy grants: a great mass of unemployed people, hungry and ill-clothed, threatens politics and even the military position. But while ships are critically needed for operations the heads of state have approved, none may be diverted to separate national import programs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d381:
Oil and shipping fill the Joint Chiefs' session at Yalta on February 8, 1945, recorded in these minutes. The chiefs first took up levels of supply of petroleum products in all theaters. Then came an overall review of cargo and troop shipping for the rest of 1945. Admiral Leahy noted the report was agreed by the shipping boards.

Leahy observed, dryly, that its essence was an agreement to study the question again when need arose. General Somervell answered that the need had already arisen. Redeployment plans, above all, had outrun the paper. The minutes show the alliance's scarcest asset — hulls — being argued over to the last conference week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d481:
All three powers have now approved the basic texts for Germany, Ambassador Winant cabled from London on February 6, 1945. The Soviet acting member of the European Advisory Commission had told him that Moscow approved the protocol on zones of occupation. It also approved the agreement on control machinery.

With that word, the three founding texts stood approved without reserve. They were the instrument of unconditional surrender, the zones protocol, and the control machinery agreement. Winant's short cable closes talks that had run in London for over a year. Yalta could build on settled paper; the rulebook for ruling Germany existed before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d81:
General Jacob Devers, commanding the Sixth Army Group, warned General Marshall on June 20, 1945, that the Berlin survey party was still blocked. His telegram from Frankfurt is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Every attempt to get Soviet permission for General Parks to enter Berlin had failed.

Antonov in Moscow would not agree to Parks entering before June 28 or 29, Devers reports. He judges it highly unlikely that proper arrangements for the conference could be finished by the scheduled date if work starts that late. olcott-buddhist-catechism-1881:
Henry Steel Olcott taught the faith of the Buddha to the young in A Buddhist Catechism, his slim book of 1881. Olcott had moved to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. He found schools there taught by faiths not of the isle. He wrote this guide to set the faith in plain words for its own youth.

Short asks meet short replies, in the mode of faith schools of the West. Heads of the faith on the isle passed the text as true. Schools there used it for years. Olcott is still held dear on the isle. The guide went through scores of print runs in its long life. Few books by a man of the West have shaped schools of the East so.
tyndall-floating-matter-air-1881:
John Tyndall, an Irish man of physics who worked in London, set out these essays in 1881. His theme is the fine dust that floats in the air around us. The work grew from his clash with Henry Bastian over the birth of life.

With a beam of light, Tyndall could see dust in air and tell when air was pure. He showed that pure air starts no rot and no growth in sealed broths at all. His proof backed Pasteur in England and shut the case on life from rot.
michelson-relative-motion-ether-1881:
Albert A. Michelson, a young American physicist, ran this first ether test at Potsdam in 1881. He sought to catch the Earth in its flight through the ether. If the ether stood still, light should race at changed speeds as the Earth moved.

He built a fine tool that split a light beam and sent the parts on two paths. The beams came back with no shift at all, though his maths said a shift must show. The blank result was the first crack in the ether scheme, and it puzzled the field for years.
abbott-primitive-industry-1881:
Charles Conrad Abbott, a doctor and keen digger in New Jersey, wrote this book on the Trenton gravels in 1881. He had found rough stone tools in the gravel beds near the Delaware River. The finds led him to a bold claim for the age of man in America.

Abbott held that the tools came from a true stone age race in America, as old as Europe's. His claim was the first of its kind for the New World, made in full print. Later men, led by Hrdlicka, took his proof apart stone by stone in the years that came.
geikie-prehistoric-europe-1881:
James Geikie, a Scots rock scholar, wrote this sketch of the ice age and man's place in it in 1881. Its full theme is the rocks of Europe in the time before writ history. Geikie knew the signs of old ice work in the field at first hand.

He reads scraped rocks, stray blocks, and gravel beds to map how far the ice sheets spread. In that cold frame he sets the stone age folk, their tools, and their beasts. The book gave the men of the stone age a firm time scale for the first time.
sbe-10-dhammapada-suttanipata-1881:
F. Max Muller built the Sacred Books of the East as a vast set of fifty books. Book Ten of the set came out in 1881. It holds two of the best loved texts of the Buddhist faith. V. Fausboll made the English dress used here.

The Dhammapada is a book of short verses on the mind, on pain, and on the path. Its lines are said to hold the core teach of the Buddha in brief form. The Sutta-Nipata holds some of the most old talks of the faith. The book is a sound first step into Buddhist texts in English.
sbe-11-buddhist-suttas-1881:
T. W. Rhys Davids gave the Buddhist Suttas English dress in 1881. The book is Book Eleven of the Sacred Books of the East. Rhys Davids was the great Pali man of his age in Britain. The texts here are talks said to come from the Buddha himself.

The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells of the last days and death of the Buddha. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is his first preach, the turn of the wheel of law. More talks deal with marks of a true priest and the snares of false views. The book is a core set of texts for the faith.
sbe-13-vinaya-texts-1-1881:
T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg gave the Vinaya Texts English dress in 1881. The work is Book Thirteen of the Sacred Books of the East. Part One of the Vinaya holds the core rules for monks of the Buddha. The Vinaya is the rule book of the monk host.

The Patimokkha lists the rules a monk must own to, month by month. The Mahavagga, Books One to Four, tells how the order was formed and how new monks join. Tales of the first monks frame the dry lists of rules. The book shows the monk life as the faith first set it down.
france-crime-sylvestre-bonnard-1881:
Anatole France published The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard in 1881, his first novel, Englished here in 1906. The English translation of 1906 gives an elderly scholar's gentle, ironic adventures among books and a young ward. France's limpid irony and love of old Paris announce the master stylist of the next forty years.

Bonnard, a member of the Institute, hunts a rare manuscript to Sicily and into a bookseller's clutches in Paris. He rescues Jeanne, the granddaughter of his lost love, from a cruel guardian and a boarding school's neglect. To give her a dowry he sells his library, and the crime of the title is a kindly theft. The close finds the old scholar content, his books gone and his ward happily wed in Paris. The novel's charm and humane skepticism won France his first wide public in France.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-2-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 2 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume moves from Constantine to Julian and the later 300s. Christianity triumphs as the state religion, and Gibbon tells the story with unmatched irony. Councils, heresies, and imperial courts crowd the pages.

Julian the Apostate, who tried to restore the old gods, receives a rich portrait. Gibbon also treats the rise of monastic life and the Goths pressing on the frontiers. His footnotes mix deep learning with dry wit. Readers prized the volume for both narrative and character sketches. The History was becoming the standard against which English histories were judged.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-3-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 3 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume runs from Theodosius to the fall of the Western Empire in 476. Barbarian invasions, court intrigue, and religious strife fill the story. Attila and the Huns sweep across Europe in famous chapters.

The sack of Rome by Goths and Vandals marks the end of an age. Gibbon treats saints and emperors with the same cool, ironic eye. His account of the last Roman emperors is both sad and scornful. The volume closes the Western story while the East endures. Gibbon's grand design now spans a thousand years. Its scale still awes historians.
darwin-vegetable-mould-1881:
Charles Darwin spent his last years studying small things close to home at Down House in Kent. His final book, published in 1881, reports forty years of watching earthworms turn soil. He had first read a short paper on worms to a learned society back in 1837. Few readers expected worms to fill a bestseller, yet the book sold fast.

Darwin shows that worms drag leaves below ground, swallow earth, and cast it up as fine mould. Inch by inch, he argues, they bury stones, ruins, and whole fields under new soil. The book is a quiet proof that slow, small forces can reshape the land.
hallywell-melampronoea-1681:
Henry Hallywell was a Cambridge scholar and clergyman whose Melampronoea appeared in 1681. The Greek title names his subject: a discourse of the polity and kingdom of darkness. He wrote in reply to John Webster, who had doubted the reality of spirits.

Hallywell defends the reality of spirits against the mechanical philosophy then rising in the Royal Society's circle. If matter and motion explain all, he warns, then soul, providence, and moral rule dissolve with the ghosts. The book catches the moment when England's learned men fought over whether the unseen world existed at all. His fear was pastoral as much as learned: a world without spirits leaves souls unguarded.
holmes-common-law-1881:
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr published The Common Law in 1881, from lectures given in Boston. Holmes, a Civil War veteran soon to be a judge, was not yet forty. The book made his name and began a long shift in American legal thought.

Holmes opened with his famous line: the life of the law has not been logic, it has been experience. He traced crime, torts, and contracts from old Germanic and Roman roots to modern rules, showing law shaped by policy and need. Judges, he argued, make law while claiming only to find it. The book is read as a founding text of American legal realism and of Holmes's own road to the Supreme Court.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-1-188:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage edited Volume 1 of History of Woman Suffrage, published in 1881. The leaders of the movement wrote its history themselves, from records they had kept. Volume 1 covers the years from 1848 to 1861.

Speeches, letters, convention reports, and newspaper accounts trace the movement from the Seneca Falls convention of 1848 to the Civil War. The editors printed documents at length so later readers could judge the record directly. Their version favors their own wing of the movement, a point later historians note. Still, the volume is the documentary record of the American women's movement by the women who led it, and a basic source ever since.
dryden-absalom-achitophel-1681:
John Dryden, England's poet laureate, wrote Absalom and Achitophel in 1681 during a fight over the royal succession. Catholics were barred from the throne, and some Protestants wanted the king's son Monmouth to inherit instead. Dryden answered with a satire in biblical dress, published anonymously.

King Charles becomes David, Monmouth becomes his beloved son Absalom, and the scheming Earl of Shaftesbury becomes the tempter Achitophel. Dryden praises his friends and shreds his enemies in polished heroic couplets. The poem is a masterclass in political satire: elegant, funny, and ruthless. It helped define the form for the next century of English verse.
rossetti-ballads-sonnets-1881:
Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a painter as well as a poet, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. Ballads and Sonnets, published in 1881, was his last book, appearing a year before his death. It completes the long sonnet sequence he had worked on for decades.

The House of Life here reaches its full 101 sonnets, tracing love, loss, and memory across a lifetime. The ballads include The King's Tragedy, a dark tale of James I of Scotland's murder, told with dramatic force. Rossetti's language is rich, musical, and steeped in medieval color. The volume sealed his place as the central poet of the Pre-Raphaelite circle.
schiller-robbers-1781:
Friedrich Schiller was twenty-one when The Robbers burst onto the German stage in 1781. Alexander Fraser Tytler translated the play into English in 1792. Karl Moor, cheated of his inheritance by his brother Franz, takes to the forest as captain of a robber band.

Karl's rage at a corrupt world drives him to crimes he cannot undo. Franz, cold and scheming, plots to seize the estate and their father's love. The old count and the faithful Amalia stand between the brothers' storm. Schiller wrote with the heat of the Sturm und Drang movement behind him. The play made him famous overnight and set a pattern for European melodrama.
bjornson-arne-anderson-1881:
Rasmus B. Anderson translated Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Arne and early tales for Houghton Mifflin in 1881 and 1882. Bjørnson, later a Nobel laureate, built modern Norwegian prose from peasant life. Arne, the title tale, follows a crofter's son torn between his father's violence, his mother's songs, and his own longing to leave the valley.

Other sketches in the volume give brides, fishermen, and small farms in Bjørnson's fresh, direct manner. He wrote against the stiff book language of his day, close to living speech. Anderson, himself of Norwegian stock, made these tales a bridge between Norway and America. The volume helped found a national literature and export it at once. Bjørnson's peasants entered world reading through doors like this one.
cyril-five-tomes-against-nestorius-pusey:
Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, led the attack on Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople who split Christ into two sons in his preaching. His Five Tomes Against Nestorius answer the rival book by book. Edward Bouverie Pusey translated them for the Library of the Fathers in 1881, with Cyril's Scholia on the Incarnation and other pieces.

Cyril defends one Christ, true God and true man in a single person, and the title Mother of God for Mary. The fight came to a head at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which cast Nestorius out. Pusey's volume gives the winning side in its own strong words. It is a core text of the Christological debates.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol5-1881:
Volume V of the Guiding Symptoms came out in 1881, printed after Hering's death from his stored notes. The series gathers proven signs for hundreds of remedies, and this middle volume keeps the alphabetical march going. Headings split every entry by region, organ, and function.

Small marks beside a symptom carry the real craft of the set. They tell the reader which signs showed up again and again, and which ones cured in practice. Without them the pages would be a flood; with them a working doctor could find a remedy's keynote fast, even mid-consultation.
nordenskiold-voyage-vega-vol2-1881:
Volume Two of the Vega voyage completes the first transit of the Northeast Passage. The English edition appeared in 1881, before the first volume. Nordenskiöld's ship had wintered within sight of her goal, held by the ice for ten months.

In July 1879 the Vega broke free and passed into the Pacific, to worldwide applause. The return sail visits Japan, China, and Ceylon, then home through Suez to a hero's welcome in Stockholm. Scientific results fill the closing chapters: charts, fossils, and notes on Arctic peoples. The voyage proved Asia could be circled by sea, a dream since the 1500s.
plos-pone-0003381:
Dru S. Dace and colleagues studied abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye in 2008. Such growth, called neovascularization, is a common cause of blindness. The team focused on interleukin-10, a signal that usually calms immune responses. They asked how it acts when a young eye is starved of oxygen.

Mice lacking the signal grew far fewer of the harmful new vessels. The signal seemed to steer how immune cells called macrophages react to low oxygen. With that steering gone, the vessel growth slowed down. The work names a surprising driver of eye disease and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0003481:
Yongjun Guan and co-authors found T cells shielding themselves from HIV in this 2008 paper. CD4 T cells are the main target of HIV infection. Some T cells release chemicals that block the viral doorway CCR5. Those chemicals can guard nearby cells from R5 virus strains.

The twist here is protection of the producing cell itself. Individual CD4 cells making those ligands defended their own surface. Such self-protection may let some cells resist infection from within. Understanding it could inspire therapies that copy the trick. Cells that guard themselves may also seed the viral reservoir that resists cure.
plos-pone-0003581:
Jindong Chen and co-authors removed a kidney gene in mice for this 2008 study. Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is an inherited cancer syndrome. Its gene, FLCN, was found by positional cloning and acts as a tumor suppressor. Mutations cause kidney cancers, skin growths, and lung cysts.

Mice lacking FLCN in the kidney developed polycystic kidneys. They also developed renal neoplasia, abnormal kidney growths. The model confirms the gene's tumor suppressor role in living tissue. It gives researchers a system for studying this rare syndrome. Kidney tumors in this syndrome tend to grow slowly but return over time.
plos-pone-0003681:
Patricia Renesto, Clarisse Rovery, Jacques Schrenzel, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever and reaches people through tick bites. The skin sore at the bite, called an eschar, is where infection begins. The team read the bacterium's gene activity there.

They profiled which genes the bacterium switches on inside the eschar. That snapshot shows what the germ does first, while it is still at the entry point. Knowing those early moves can help explain how the infection spreads from skin to the rest of the body.
plos-pone-0003781:
Jasna Martinovic, Thomas Gruber, and Matthias M. Müller published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Recognizing an object means binding its separate features into one thing. Early steps of that process are thought to code features very fast, in distinct groups of neurons. Conjunctions of features come later.

The authors recorded brain activity while people processed visual objects. They compared how single features and feature combinations are coded in the human brain. The work probes the first steps by which scattered visual features turn into objects we can name and use.
plos-pone-0003881:
Marta Coll, Simone Libralato, Sergi Tudela, and co-authors assessed ocean fishing in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Fishing removes mass and energy from the sea in every catch landed. That loss can no longer feed the higher levels of the food web. The authors call heavy removal of that kind ecosystem overfishing.

The paper weighs how much production fishing takes from marine food webs. It looks past single fish stocks to the whole system that supports them. The argument helps managers judge when total catch harms the wider ocean. It gives a frame for setting limits that protect more than one target species.
plos-pone-0003981:
Jayne Byakika-Tusiime, Leslie W. Chinn, Jessica H. Oyugi, and co-authors compared generic and brand HIV drugs in 2008. Generic therapy is the mainstay of HIV care in poor settings. Little proof existed that generics match brand drugs in the body. The team compared three drugs used together in Uganda.

Their PLOS ONE article measured steady-state drug levels in HIV-infected adults. The drugs were stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine. Matching levels support bioequivalence of the generic and innovator versions. Such proof underpins confidence in low-cost treatment programs worldwide. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004081:
Hayate Merad, Horea Porumb, Loussiné Zargarian, and co-authors examined HIV's DNA-inserting enzyme in 2009. Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host cell's DNA. That step makes HIV infection permanent in the cell. The team studied the enzyme's catalytic core structure.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies an unusual helix-turn-helix motif in that core. Spanning residues 149 to 186, it binds viral DNA and LEDGF. LEDGF is a host protein that guides integration. A defined binding motif offers a target for drugs blocking integration. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004181:
Junwei Yang and colleagues published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bleeding in the lungs is a major and often deadly feature of severe leptospirosis. Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caught from animal-contaminated water, and the cause of its lung bleeding is unclear. The dangerous serovar Lai of Leptospira interrogans makes a protein that acts on platelet-activating factor, a blood signal.

Following that clue, the team measured the activity of the matching enzyme, PAF acetylhydrolase, in patients' blood. They propose its serum activity as a possible clinical marker for the lung bleeding form of the disease. An early warning marker could help doctors spot the patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0004281:
Sarah Parker and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is central to its success as a pathogen, and mycolic acids are key components of that wall. The genes that join the wall's building blocks sit in a cluster running from Rv3799c through at least Rv3804c.

The team characterised one gene in that cluster, Rv3802c. They report that it encodes a phospholipase and thioesterase, and that the antimycobacterial agent tetrahydrolipstatin inhibits it. An enzyme in the wall-building line that a drug can block is a lead for new tuberculosis treatments.
plos-pone-0004381:
Heads in backboned animals are built from two cell groups working side by side. Skull parts, tendons, and connective tissue come from neural crest cells. Most head muscles come from a second group, the cranial mesoderm. Julien Grenier, Marie-Aimée Teillet, Raphaëlle Grifone, and co-authors studied how the two groups relate. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier work showed crest cells migrate in close company with mesoderm cells. The authors traced that pairing during head muscle growth in the embryo. Their aim was to map who builds what, and how the groups interact. The map helps explain normal face and jaw formation. It also frames birth defects where those tissues form wrong.
plos-pone-0004481:
Age and food change which genes are active in dog muscle, report Ingmar Middelbos, Brittany Vester, Lisa Karr-Lilienthal, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team read gene activity in the thigh muscle of beagles using gene chips. Twelve female dogs took part: six aged one year and six aged twelve years, fed one of two test diets.

By comparing young and old dogs on each diet, the study separates the marks of aging from the marks of food. Genes that shift with age alone hint at how muscle weakens over time. Genes that shift with diet show where food can push back. Dogs age faster than people, so their muscle offers a sped-up view of changes that also matter for human aging and diet advice.
plos-pone-0004581:
A new antibody test measures hepcidin, the body's iron gatekeeper hormone, in human blood, report Vasiliki Koliaraki, Martha Marinou, Theodoros Vassilakopoulos, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepcidin is a small peptide built from twenty-five amino acids. When it rises, iron is locked away inside storage cells, which contributes to the anemia of chronic disease. When it falls, iron deficiency and overload states follow.

Measuring hepcidin well had been a bottleneck: the peptide is small and hard to assay. The team presents a novel immunological assay for quantifying it in serum. A reliable test lets doctors separate anemia types that look alike. It also helps track iron disorders where the hormone itself is the problem.
plos-pone-0004681:
Sarosh Fatakia, Stefano Costanzi, and Carson Chow used math tools to find linked spots in key drug targets, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The targets are a huge family of cell surface proteins that sense signals. They are the most common targets of drugs in use today.

Some spots in these proteins change together over time, which hints they work as a team. The team used shared change scores and graph methods to find tight groups of such spots. Knowing which spots move as a group can guide drug design. It can also help predict how a change in one spot affects the whole protein.
plos-pone-0004781:
Lionel Nowak and Pascal Barone showed that contrast adaptation helps keep orientation tuning steady in primate visual cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Single neurons keep the same preferred orientation whether a pattern is faint or bold. Past studies used long stimulus times, which left room for adaptation to shape the result during each trial.

The team used shorter, controlled exposures in primate V1 cells. They found adaptation to contrast does help hold tuning width steady. Steady tuning lets the brain read shape regardless of light level. The work refines models of early vision. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
green-making-of-england-1881:
Anglo-Saxon England takes shape in Green's The Making of England, from 1881. English settlers cross the sea and carve kingdoms from Roman Britain's ruins. Missionaries then bring the Christian faith, and Alfred the Great defends the land against Danish invasion.

Green taught Victorian readers where their country truly came from. He writes of plowmen and monks beside kings and war bands. Settlement, conversion, and learning form his triple theme throughout. The book's humane warmth set it apart from drier chronicles of the age. It remains a beloved account of England's birth, written for the people whose story it tells.
nasir-khusraw-sefer-nameh-schefer-1881:
Nasir-i Khusraw walked the Islamic world for seven years, and Charles Schefer's 1881 French version carries his Sefer Nameh to Western readers. The Persian traveler went from Central Asia to Mecca, Jerusalem, and Cairo. His precise, curious eye notes cities, shrines, markets, and roads along the whole vast way.

He measures walls, counts gates, and tastes local bread with equal care. Few travel books of the medieval Islamic world match its freshness. Faith and wonder guide his steps, yet fact fills his pages. The record stands as the finest travel account of its age and region, in a French dress that served scholars for generations.
petit-albert-1881:
Household magic fills Le veritable petit Albert, in this 1881 printing of the great French folk grimoire. Secrets promise help with health, love, luck, and protection for ordinary folk. For three centuries the Petit Albert ranked among France's best-selling books of hidden knowledge, thumbed in farms and villages across the land.

Recipes, charms, and wonders pass from hand to hand in its pages. Joseph-Norbert Duquet's printing carried the old lore to new buyers here. Scholars trace its roots to the secrets ascribed to Albert the Great. The people's magic, plain and practical, survives in this little book, endlessly reprinted because readers kept finding their needs in it.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol4-1881:
The fourth volume of Twiss's Bracton came out in 1881, continuing the Rolls Series text of the great thirteenth-century treatise. Bracton wrote as a royal justice who knew the courts from inside. His book ordered the whole of English law, and Twiss's edition spread that order across six volumes.

Volume 4 takes up the criminal side of the law, the pleas of the crown. It covers felonies such as homicide, theft, and arson, and how the king's justice pursued them. Trial by jury was still young, and Bracton shows older proofs giving way to newer practice. The common law appears here at its sternest, with death or outlawry waiting for many offenses. The volume is a prime source for the birth of English criminal law.
coke-institutes-part2-1681:
The Second Part of Coke's Institutes appeared in print in 1681, decades after its author's death in 1634. Coke had written it as an exposition of the great statutes of England. Parliament ordered the later parts published during the civil war era, when his authority served the cause against the crown.

Above all, the volume expounds Magna Carta clause by clause, treating the charter as England's fundamental law. Coke reads old words broadly, finding in them guards for liberty, property, and fair trial. His commentary became the arsenal from which seventeenth-century lawyers drew their arguments against royal power. American founders later drank from the same source. The book taught generations that even kings stand under a law they did not make.
pothier-traite-contrat-de-vente-1781:
Robert Joseph Pothier's Treatise on the Contract of Sale, printed in French in this 1781 edition, is a classic of French private law. Pothier, a judge at Orléans, wrote a series of treatises that ordered the whole law of obligations. The sale contract, the most common deal in daily life, got his fullest care.

He defines what a sale is, what may be sold, the duties of buyer and seller, and the remedies when goods or payment fail. His clarity is the marvel: hard cases dissolve under his plain distinctions. When the drafters of Napoleon's Civil Code needed a guide, they drew on Pothier more than on any other writer. The treatise thus taught France its private law, and its influence reached Louisiana and Quebec as well.
cia-0000007481:
Winter 1962 brought volume 6, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's internal journal for working officers. One named piece, Anatomy of Spying, signals the issue's focus on how espionage actually works. The journal circulated inside the agency rather than to the public.

Inside, practitioners wrote for each other about tradecraft, analysis, and the hard parts of secret work. Such writing helped a young agency turn field experience into shared lessons. Released decades later, the issue lets outsiders watch that training process. It is primary evidence for how the early Cold War CIA understood its own trade.
cia-0000008381:
Plans for the Tan-Zam Railway drew CIA attention in an October 1965 paper on the project's prospects. The line was meant to link landlocked Zambia to the sea through Tanzania, easing its reliance on routes south. China backed the scheme, which made it a Cold War contest as well as a railway.

The paper weighs whether the line would be built and what it would change. Railways in such studies stand for trade, loyalty, and reach, not just track and trains. Readers see Beijing's growing role in Africa judged from Washington. The file captures development politics at an early Cold War turning point.
cia-0000008881:
Iran's current crisis, as of February 1951, is the subject of a CIA paper from the oil dispute's first heat. Iran's parliament was moving to take over the British-owned oil industry, and nationalist feeling ran high. The shah's authority and the government's stability both looked shaky.

The paper weighs the players: court, parliament, street, and foreign powers with oil at stake. Two years later, a coup backed by Washington and London would end the crisis by force. Reading the 1951 analysis shows the problem as first framed. It is a prelude written before anyone in the file names the ending.
cia-0000009081:
Peru's prospects came before CIA analysts in a paper dated June 1965. President Fernando Belaunde's government was pushing reforms while facing economic strain and stirrings of guerrilla unrest in the Andes. Washington watched Peru as one front in a wider Latin American contest.

The paper weighs the government's strength, the opposition, and the chances of upheaval. Country studies like this one tried to warn of crises before they broke. Peru did fall to a military coup three years later, which gives the analysis edge. Readers can measure the analysts' judgment against what actually followed in Lima.
cia-0000009681:
Two American prisoners held by the North Vietnamese Army were sighted in the Prey Ve area, a May 1972 report states. The place name is cut short in the heading, which places the sighting in the Cambodian border region. North Vietnamese units operated widely inside Cambodia by 1972.

Prisoners in NVA hands inside Cambodia fell between two countries' records. Officials in Saigon and Washington both had reason to track them, and neither had easy access. A dated sighting at least fixed the men's survival to that spring. The file preserves it as one more point in the borderland captivity record of the war.
cia-0000009981:
An American pilot died in the crash of an L-19 reconnaissance plane in Vinh Binh province, an October 1972 report states. The L-19 Bird Dog was a small, slow spotter plane whose crews flew low over battlefields. Vinh Binh lies in the Mekong Delta's flat, wet south.

Bird Dog crews directed artillery and strikes, work that kept them over enemy guns daily. Their losses were steady and their planes left little wreckage to find. A confirmed death in a Delta crash closed one such crewman's case. The file honors the spotter war's risk with a plain provincial record.
cia-0000010581:
North Africa's current situation is surveyed in an August 1952 CIA paper. France then ruled Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia as protectorates or territory, and nationalist movements pressed in all three. Egypt, newly under its Free Officers after the July 1952 revolution, watched from the east.

The survey weighs French control against rising demands for independence across the Maghreb. Washington was torn between its French ally and the region's clear direction. Within a decade every territory named was independent, Algeria through a brutal war. This file catches the old order's last calm, surveyed whole in the summer of 1952.
cia-0000010881:
In February 1951 the CIA judged how three Southeast Asian lands might stand up to communist pressure: Thailand, Burma, and Malaya. China had just fallen to Mao's forces, and Washington feared the region could topple country by country. Malaya was already fighting a communist revolt under British rule, while Burma faced revolts of its own.

The paper grades each country's will and strength to resist, one by one. It treats their governments, armies, and rebel movements as the front line of a wider contest. Written before America's deep plunge into Vietnam, it shows the early map of fears that shaped later policy.
cia-0000012281:
Ed Proctor and Jack Smith, two American officials, talked over the use of material called Chickadee in May 1961, and a CIA record preserves their conversation. Chickadee was a cover name for sensitive source material in the Penkovsky case. The question before the men was how such material could be used without exposing the man who supplied it.

The record shows the home front's paperwork: coordination, caution, and argument inside the government. Running a great source took as much care in Washington as in Moscow. For readers, the page reveals the handling rules that protected secrets and source alike.
cia-0000012381:
Military Thought, the Soviet armed forces' journal, might be declassified, and an October 1965 paper weighs the considerations. The agency had gathered the journal's issues through channels tied to the Penkovsky years. Its articles, written by Soviet generals for each other, had been mined in secret for what they revealed about doctrine and plans.

Releasing such material meant judging what secrecy still protected. The paper balances the gains of openness against the habits of classification. For readers, it shows open-source gold being weighed: the foe's own words, and the question of who else might read them.
cia-0000012481:
Six American pilots were held in a two-story building in Sam Neua, Laos, and a CIA report from July 1967 records the fact in detail. Sam Neua was the Pathet Lao's stronghold country in the northeast. The report describes the captives' circumstances: the building's layout, the guards' routines, and the conditions the men lived under, as sources on the ground reported them.

Such detail made the intelligence believable and usable. Rescue planning and family accounting both began from facts like these. For readers, the report is architectural witness: a prison's address, known and written down.
cia-0000014781: Communist reaction to the Rosenberg execution in Uruguay fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1953. The executions had taken place on June 19 in New York. Reaction files flowed in from capitals around the world that summer. Uruguay's entry shows the case echoing even in countries far from the main stage. The Uruguay reaction file rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015281: Unknown flying objects were seen over Budapest, in a CIA report dated March 1, 1957. Budapest had risen in revolt the fall before and been crushed. Reports from a watched capital carried weight beyond the sighting itself. The file adds Hungary's sky to the eastern bloc sightings the agency gathered. The Budapest report is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015381: An interview with a deleted name fills a CIA file dated September 4, 1955. No topic survives in the clipped title at all. Such a file can be logged but barely described from outside. It stands in the record as proof a talk took place, with its heart cut away by the censor's hand.
cia-0000037481:
American prisoners and missing men in Laos are the subject of a CIA record dated June 2, 1968, tied to the JPRC. The JPRC was the Joint Personnel Recovery Center, which worked to rescue and account for men in Southeast Asia. Laos was its hardest field, since the war there was secret.

Inside, the file concerns the center's Laos cases: who was held, who was missing, and what was known. Recovery work in Laos faced jungles, enemy forces, and official silence at once. The record shows the organization built for that work, and the scale of the task it faced in a country where little could be said aloud.
cia-0000041181:
Talks to prisoners of war, attributed to Jane Fonda, were broadcast from North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated June 5, 1972. The broadcasts aimed her words at the men held in Hanoi's prisons. Speaking to prisoners was the most charged part of her whole visit.

Inside, the attributed talks are preserved as the monitors heard them. Prisoners who heard such broadcasts faced them from inside cells and camps. The file records how the visit reached its sharpest point. A famous American voice was carried into the prisons, and the men there had no choice about hearing it from their captors.
cia-0000042781:
Further reportage on the Jesuit assassinations fills a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. The November date places this file weeks into the case's public life. By then the murders had become a fixed point in the war's story.

Inside, the reporting continues, with the case still drawing daily coverage. Sustained reportage kept pressure on every party to the war. Governments could outwait a single headline. They could not so easily outwait a story that returned each day with fresh detail and fresh anger. The file preserves that persistence, which helped make the priests' case the best known crime of the Salvadoran war.
cia-0000042881:
El Salvador faced human rights concerns, in a CIA record dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog. The title ties the account to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Concerns was the polite word for a grim and growing list.

Inside, the pressures on the country over its rights record are surveyed. Reports from churches and rights groups fed the case against it. American aid debates turned on those reports each session. The file shows a small country cornered by its own record. The autumn's killings were about to make that record far harder to defend.
cia-0000045981: Handwriting specialists weighed in on the claimed prisoner photograph and on samples of writing, and a CIA item dated June 1, 1991, kept their comments. Graphology, the study of handwriting, was one of several tests thrown at the evidence that summer. The item shows the missing-men hunt reaching for any tool that might settle a claim.
cia-0000049281: A status report on El Salvador from 1980 fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Status reports were the baseline genre: where the country stood, in the writer's judgment, that season. This one catches the country in the civil war's first year, before the lines hardened into a decade's shape.
cia-0000049381: The Situation in Central America is the broad heading of declassified CIA document 0000049381, dated February 5, 1989. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper surveys the region as a whole. Its generality is the point to note: It is a single dated overview item rather than a country study. The agency kept it as part of its closing-years reporting on Central America.
cia-0000096481: An untitled document about no independence for British Guiana is declassified CIA document 0000096481, dated September 5, 1964. plos-pone-0005381:
Cancer therapy needs agents that find tumors in the body and mark them for imaging or attack. Cuesta and colleagues built such an agent, a trivalent antibody fragment they call a trimerbody, and tested it in living animals in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The trimerbody joins a single-chain antibody fragment to a collagen-derived section that holds three arms together. Three binding arms grip tumor targets more firmly than one. In vivo tests showed the engineered fragments target tumors and support imaging, a step toward clinical scanners. Three arms cost more to make than one, so the gain must be real in the body. Not just in a dish, and the live tests here are the ones that count for that claim.
plos-pone-0005481:
David Schley, Simon Gubbins, and David Paton weighed the risks of local movement bans in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Foot-and-mouth disease can sweep through farm animals, so countries guard their disease-free status with care. When an outbreak is found, officials often ban animal movements nearby.

The authors asked how wide and how long such bans need to be, given the risk that infection has already spread. Bans protect herds but also halt trade and farm work. A clear view of the risk helps officials choose bans that stop disease without needless harm to farming areas.
plos-pone-0005581:
Mascha van 't Wout and co-authors studied social cue reading in schizophrenia in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People read others' gaze and body motion quickly and without effort. That skill underlies smooth social life.

People with schizophrenia often struggle socially, and weak reading of basic cues may be part of the cause. The team used a new visual illusion to test quick, automatic attention to social signals in patients and in people at high risk. Gaps on such a basic test could help spot risk early. Quick cue reading can be tested without language, which makes the illusion useful across patient groups.
plos-pone-0005681:
Kevin Chen, Jonas Maaskola, Mark Siegal, and co-authors rechecked a popular tool for predicting microRNA targets in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA bits that tune gene activity by binding to messenger RNA. The PITA program scores targets by binding strength and by how open the site is.

Using population gene data from fruit flies, the team tested whether PITA's calls hold up. They found the program was less precise than its first report claimed. That gap matters, because labs spend months chasing predicted targets. A sharper test of prediction tools keeps that work aimed at sites most likely to be real.
plos-pone-0005781:
Anésia Santos and co-authors studied in 2009 how a plant defense receptor fine-tunes its own activation. The receptor NIK1 is a target of a virus protein that shuts down the plant's antiviral alarm. NIK1 belongs to a family of receptor-like kinases that guard cell surfaces.

The team found NIK1 adds phosphate tags to its activation loop in a step-by-step pattern. Single threonine spots in that loop play different roles in the kinase's power. Mapping those steps shows how the antiviral signal is dialed up. Plant viruses and their hosts are locked in an arms race, and the loop is one contested dial.
plos-pone-0006381:
Low oxygen in tumors pushes cancer cells toward a mobile, spreading state. Ingrid Moen and colleagues gave hyperbaric oxygen to rats with mammary tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Tumor hypoxia is relevant for growth, metabolism, and the transition that lets cells migrate.

Hyperoxic treatment induced the reverse transition, from mesenchymal back to epithelial character, in the rat adenocarcinoma model. Settled cells spread less readily than mobile ones. Oxygen therapy thus did more than feed tissue; it changed tumor identity. The result supports studying oxygen as an adjunct in cancer care.
plos-pone-0006481:
Dennis vanEngelsdorp and colleagues described colony collapse disorder in honey bees for PLOS ONE in 2009. Over two winters, large-scale losses of managed honey bee colonies in the United States had gone unexplained. No known cause fit the pattern. Beekeepers found hives empty of adult bees with food still present.

A descriptive study is the first step when a new syndrome appears. The authors set out what the disorder looks like and how cases can be defined. Clear definitions let later studies compare data across apiaries and states. The work helped organize the search for causes of a crisis for pollination and farming.
plos-pone-0006581:
Richard Piech, Jade Lewis, Caroline Parkinson, and colleagues scanned brains during food judgments in PLOS ONE in 2009. How much we desire a meal depends on both the constituent foods and how hungry we are. Not every meal becomes more desirable with increasing hunger, though. The brain therefore evaluates foods in a hunger-dependent way.

The team identified neural correlates of appetite and hunger-related evaluative judgments. Brain imaging shows which areas scale their response with hunger. Those areas are targets for understanding overeating and appetite loss. The study connects a daily experience, choosing food, to measurable brain activity.
plos-pone-0009481:
Karlee Silver and colleagues studied malaria in pregnancy in PLOS ONE in 2010. When malaria infects the placenta, babies are often born too small. Low birth weight raises the risk of death and poor health. Proteins called angiopoietins guide the growth of blood vessels in the placenta. The team measured these proteins in infected mothers.

Levels of the two main angiopoietins were out of balance where malaria was present. That upset went with lower birth weight. The link suggests that broken vessel growth is one path from infection to harm. Guarding those vessel signals could be a way to protect unborn children.
plos-pone-0009581:
Carl Soulsbury compared mating and fatherhood across mammals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Larger testes are read as a sign of stronger sperm competition between males. In some groups, social mating systems match that pattern well. In others, the match is poor. Soulsbury gathered data on testes size, mating systems, and who actually fathers the young across mammal species.

The study tests whether size alone predicts real paternity patterns. Genetic fatherhood data give a firmer check than social labels do. Results of this kind refine a classic claim in evolution. They show where a simple body measure works as a guide, and where it misleads.
plos-pone-0009681:
Cytomegalovirus is a common virus that can hide in the body for life. Christopher Snyder and colleagues asked in 2010 how the immune system first learns to attack it. They worked with a mouse form of the virus. The mutant strain could infect cells but could not spread between them.

Even with spread blocked, the crippled virus primed most of the virus-specific killer T cells. The priming worked through cross-presentation, where one cell shows pieces of the virus to T cells. That result shows the immune system does not need a fully spreading infection to build strong defenses.
plos-pone-0010481:
Yasuhiro Matsuo and Tetsu Kamitani reported a Parkinson's-linked protein inside melanoma tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma causes most skin cancer deaths worldwide. Parkinson's disease involves loss of brain cells and is tied to a protein called alpha-synuclein. Population studies had noticed the two diseases occur together more than chance allows. The team asked whether the brain protein shows up in melanoma.

Finding alpha-synuclein in melanoma tissue gives the population link a physical clue. Shared proteins might mean shared pathways between nerve decay and skin cancer. That could open odd but useful treatment ideas across fields. It also warns that drugs for one disease may affect the other. The study connects two specialties that rarely talk.
plos-pone-0010581:
Dawei Gou and colleagues studied gene silencing in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells can switch genes off by adding small chemical marks to DNA, a process called methylation. In flies, most marking was thought to happen early, before hatching.

The team found that a protein named SETDB1 keeps methylation going after the embryo stage. Without it, marks faded and some silent genes became active. So the same system that sets up the pattern also maintains it through later life. The result widens the known role of SETDB1 in keeping the genome stable.
plos-pone-0010681:
Lindsay Edwards and colleagues measured muscle energy use in climbers on Everest, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Thin air at high altitude starves the body of oxygen. Healthy climbers offer a clean way to study low-oxygen stress without disease muddying the picture. The work was part of the Caudwell Xtreme Everest trip.

A scan method that tracks phosphorus in muscle showed how energy stores were spent and refilled. After time at altitude, muscle handling of energy had changed in clear ways. The shifts help explain weakness at altitude. They also model what happens in patients whose lungs or blood fail to deliver enough oxygen.
plos-pone-0010781:
Tricia Petruney and colleagues mapped who holds influence over HIV prevention policy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Voluntary contraception by women living with HIV prevents more infant infections, at lower cost, than drug regimens alone. Yet prevention programs still focus almost wholly on drugs for mother-to-child transmission.

The team charted key officials, funders, and advocates and asked their views. Support for contraception as prevention was broader than expected, but a few gatekeepers held back wider adoption. Knowing exactly whose minds must change turns a vague advocacy hope into a list of meetings. The study treats influence itself as data for saving lives.
plos-pone-0010881:
Dmitri Chilov, Natalia Sinjushina, Jonna Saarimäki-Vire and co-authors published this mouse development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Beta-catenin is a protein with two jobs: it relays signals from the Wnt family of growth cues and it helps hold cells together. The team studied what happens when beta-catenin is locked on in the developing mouse midbrain and the segment just behind it.

Stabilizing the protein strongly raised several Wnt target genes, including Fgf8, another key patterning signal, even in other tissues such as the limb. Oddly, the Wnt1 signal itself soon fell, hinting at a self-limiting feedback loop. Front-to-back and top-to-bottom patterning of the brain region went astray in step. Chilov and colleagues show how one protein coordinates a whole signaling network that lays out the early brain.
plos-pone-0010981:
Alexander Hoare, Stephen Kerr, Kiat Ruxrungtham and co-authors published this HIV modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Access to first-line HIV treatment was expanding across Southeast Asia, but second-line drugs for patients whose virus becomes resistant were scarce. The authors built a mathematical model of a regional epidemic to forecast the hidden cost of that gap.

Their simulations show that after a decade of universal first-line treatment, up to a fifth of newly infected, untreated people could carry drug-resistant strains, depending on how fit those strains are. Adding yearly viral load testing, with real second-line therapy for those failing, cut transmitted resistance dramatically in the model. Hoare and colleagues warn that treatment scale-up without monitoring breeds the very resistance that makes HIV harder to treat.
plos-pone-0011081:
Buescher, Achberger, Amusan and colleagues published plant research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied Arabidopsis, a small plant often used in genetics labs. Different wild groups of this plant store minerals in their tissues at different levels, and the team asked whether genes explain the gap.

Comparing selected plant groups, the team linked natural gene differences to differences in mineral content. Those links point to genes that tune how plants take up and store key elements. The findings could help breed crops with better mineral value for people who eat them. They also show how wild variation can guide crop science.
plos-pone-0011181:
Zarate, Delhommeau, Wood and colleagues trained singers in PLOS ONE in 2010. The training taught people to hear very small pitch differences, finer than a normal note step. The team then measured singing accuracy and changes in brain responses after the practice.

Training improved how accurately people sang and altered brain activity tied to hearing. That shows adult brains remain flexible for sound skills with focused practice. The result supports music education with hard evidence of brain change. It may also help design training for people with hearing or speech difficulties.
plos-pone-0011281:
Rignell-Hydbom, Elfving, Ivarsson and colleagues studied womb exposure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some long lasting chlorine based pollutants pass from mother to unborn child. Using a nested case control design, the team related mothers' exposure to later type 1 diabetes in their children.

Their analysis links prenatal exposure to raised diabetes risk. That adds the womb period to the list of times when environment shapes lifelong health. The evidence backs limits on pollutants that persist in bodies for years. Protecting unborn children is a strong reason to keep such chemicals out of food chains and homes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1281:
Admiral King, commander in chief of the United States Fleet and chief of naval operations, wrote to the Navy Department on 26 July 1945. King ran the navy through the whole war. His word to his own department came from the summit's naval side.

The navy's concerns at Potsdam ran from fleets in the Pacific to the ports and coasts of the new Europe. King's message carried his direction home while he served with the team abroad. It shows the sea service's chief running his house by cable, in the same week Britain changed leaders and Japan got its terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1381:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint British and American military body, addressed President Truman and Prime Minister Churchill together on 24 July 1945. The chiefs advised both governments on the conduct of the war. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A paper from the Combined Chiefs speaks for the whole Anglo-American war machine. Sent while Churchill still held office, it reached both heads of government at Potsdam at once. Readers should note the weight of the channel: when the chiefs wrote jointly, they settled service disputes before the leaders ever saw them. This message shows the military side of the alliance reporting to its political chiefs in mid-summit.
frus-1945-50-intel-d81:
Russell, assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 3 November 1945. Russell's papers in the volume track the money and staffing of the State intelligence office. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By November the office's first glow had met the house reality: budgets are finite, and other bureaus wanted their share. An administration chief writing to the secretary about the new service marks the moment support had to be argued, not assumed. Readers can watch the mood change across Russell's papers from autumn into winter. The office that arrived in September as a prize was, by year's end, a cost to be justified like any other.
frus-1945-50-intel-d181:
"National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 7" bears the date 2 January 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 181 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d281:
Dated 2 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the National Security Council. It is document 281 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d381:
A memorandum dated 15 April 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Bohlen). It stands as document 381 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1861-d81:
A letter dated 11 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days of letters to London in a row show a desk that never cooled. Seward drove the effort abroad with his own hand on the pen. This note belongs to the dense September run that kept Adams fully briefed as autumn began. Adams could act on a brief order the day it landed, without waiting for more. Brief orders also left Adams free to spend his days in talks, not in study.
frus-1861-d181:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1861. The dispatch is document 181 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz had now held Madrid through a summer of war. His October report has the ease of a man who knows his court. It told Washington that Spain, for all its pride, showed no haste to aid the South. Spain's pride was real, but its purse and fleet were weak, and Schurz read both facts well. Both facts read well in Washington, where Spain had long been a cause of doubt.
frus-1861-d281:
A State Department letter of 8 July 1861 told Mr. Haldeman what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 281 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d81:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 18 June 1862. Congress received it as Document 81 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d181:
Document 181 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 3 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister in London, received both letters in the same mail.

When the Department split a day's orders between two letters, each usually took one topic, so the envoy could file and answer them apart. The practice swells the volume but sharpens the record. Read together, the 3 November pair shows Washington's hand at the very moment Britain weighed the French call for a truce in the war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d281:
A Dayton report dated 26 May 1862 stands as Document 281 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

That week, Stonewall Jackson's Valley campaign was alarming Washington itself, a reminder that the war could swing fast. Foreign envoys reported each swing, and ministers at home weighed them.
