Dayton's letter from Paris in late May is part of the transatlantic conversation by which two governments tried to price a war neither could predict. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d381:
On 24 January 1862 Cassius Clay wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward from St. Petersburg, in a letter printed as Document 381 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Clay was the American minister in Russia.

Clay's Russian service was ending: Simon Cameron had been named to succeed him, though Clay would return to the post in 1863. His January reports closed his first term at a friendly court. For Washington, the Russian channel's value lay in its contrast with Europe's western capitals, where sympathy for the South ran stronger. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d481:
James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 October 1862. The dispatch is Document 481 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

October reports from the Atlantic posts dealt with a war at sea that was spreading. Confederate raiders were burning American merchant ships. They did so in full view of neutral shores. Portugal's enforcement of its neutrality rules was therefore a live question in Washington. Harvey's account of Lisbon's stance fed the State Department's running brief on the cruisers. Read with Seward's instructions to the same post, his letters show a small legation doing work that touched every American shipowner trading across the Atlantic.
frus-1862-d581:
James Watson Webb received the year's last printed Brazilian order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 27 September 1862. It is Document 581 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote ten days after Antietam and five days after the emancipation order, though neither fact could shape Webb's conduct in Rio for months. The instruction still mattered. It fixed the Department's line for Brazil on the war. It also fixed the line on slavery's new place in the war. And it stated the neutral rules the Union expected in Brazilian ports. The Brazilian file ends the volume's American missions south of the equator, a thin correspondence stretched by distance over the whole geography of the war.
frus-1862-d681:
William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Blatchford again on 13 October 1862, less than three weeks after his last letter to him. The note is document 681 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Two letters in quick order point to a matter that needed more than one word from Washington.

Much of a secretary of state's mail never made the papers, yet it was saved all the same. This short run of letters shows Seward tending to a side file in the midst of a war for the Union's life. For the reader, the pair is a reminder that the printed record holds small threads as well as grand ones.
frus-1863p1-d81:
While three letters went out from London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote one of his own to Adams, on 13 February 1863. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 81 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The two men wrote blind of each other's same-day sheets, since the sea mail took ten days or more. Seward's letter set out the line Adams was to hold on the points then live. It is a neat case of how the exchange worked: not a talk, but two streams of paper that met in the files. This sheet is Washington's half of that crossed day.
frus-1863p1-d181:
The State Department's mail for London dated 4 May 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 181 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d281:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 September 1863. It is document 281 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d381:
From the British legation in Washington on 3 February 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 381 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d481:
On 27 April 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d581:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote this official letter to Secretary William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d681:
Charles Francis Adams received this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 December 1863. It is printed as document 681 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. Adams had held the London post since 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

The London mission was the most vital post the Union had abroad. From it, Adams dealt with British leaders on ships, trade, and the risk of Britain backing the South. Seward's notes told him where Washington stood. A reader gets a feel for the pace of that work. Letters came often, each one short, each one part of a long, careful effort.
plos-pbio-0020081:
Yu Zheng, Richard J. Roberts, and Simon Kasif offered a fresh view of adaptation in PLOS Biology in 2004. Most genes in bacteria change slowly. A smaller set, tied to the cell surface and to defense, changes much faster. The authors call these segmentally variable genes.

Fast change in surface parts makes sense. Those are the parts that meet the world: hosts, rivals, and attackers. By naming and sorting this class of genes, the paper gives genome readers a new lens. Stretches that vary a lot may mark where a microbe is adapting right now. That idea can guide the hunt for vaccine targets and for clues about how pathogens keep ahead of immune systems.
plos-pone-0000081:
Phillip Endicott, Mait Metspalu, Chris Stringer, and their team read ancient DNA from the Andaman Islands in PLOS ONE in 2006. The islanders' maternal lineages, traced by mitochondrial DNA, bear on how early modern humans spread through South Asia. New typing methods let the team test many markers in scarce ancient samples at once.

Their results sharpen where the Andaman lineages fit among South Asian groups. That placement supports a very early settlement of the islands by seafaring people. Each such data point helps draw the map of the great coastal migration out of Africa. The method itself, packing many tests into little DNA, serves all ancient DNA work.
plos-pone-0000181:
Sari Voutilainen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, Maarit Korhonen, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It comes from the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study in Finland. The team examined a common variant of the COMT gene, Val158Met, alongside the risk of acute coronary events and blood levels of homocysteine.

COMT breaks down stress hormones and also handles homocysteine-related chemistry, both tied to heart risk. The authors test whether the gene variant, on its own or with homocysteine levels, predicts heart events. Findings of this kind feed the long effort to sort real genetic risk factors from noise.
plos-pone-0000281:
Frank Seebacher and Shauna A. Murray published this reptile physiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Transient receptor potential ion channels are molecular sensors, some of which respond to temperature. The authors show these channels control thermoregulatory behaviour in reptiles, the basking and shade-seeking by which reptiles manage body temperature.

A reptile's behavior is its thermostat, so the sensors behind it matter. Linking TRP channels to that behavior connects a molecule to a whole-animal trait. The work helps explain how cold-blooded animals fine-tune their temperature, and how they might respond as their environments warm.
plos-pone-0000381:
André Catic and colleagues described a bacterial enzyme in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme, ElaD, is made by E. coli and belongs to the deubiquitinating proteases, enzymes that remove ubiquitin tags from proteins. In human cells, those tags mark proteins for destruction or change what they do, so enzymes that strip them off are powerful regulators.

Finding such an enzyme in a common bacterium raises questions about where it came from and what it does there. Bacteria are not thought to run a ubiquitin system like ours, so ElaD may act on the cells the bacterium infects. The paper opens a window on how microbes borrow or mimic host chemistry.
plos-pone-0000481:
João Carlos Sousa, Manuel João Costa, and Joana Almeida Palha wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was the meeting point of hormone science and computing. Hormones regulate genes across the body, switching them on and off in patterns that shift with time and tissue. Bioinformatics, the computational study of biological data, offers tools to read those patterns.

Their theme is learning one field from the other. Hormone research gives bioinformatics real problems with clinical weight. Computation gives endocrinology a way to handle genome-scale data. Papers of this kind map a collaboration rather than report a single experiment, arguing that neither field can fully read hormone action alone.
plos-pone-0000581:
Simone Lemeer and colleagues took a census of enzyme action in growing zebrafish, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzymes are protein-tyrosine kinases, switches that embryos use to pass signals. The team profiled their action in embryos where one chosen kinase had been knocked down, turned low.

Census work like this counts what enzymes do, not just whether they are present. When one switch is dimmed, others may pick up the slack, and that response maps the web. Zebrafish embryos are clear and grow fast, which suits this kind of work. The lessons reach cancer drugs, many of which aim at these same switches.
plos-pone-0000681:
Yong-Gang Yao, Hans-Jürgen Bandelt and Neal S. Young warned about contamination in single-cell mitochondrial DNA work, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many medical papers report mtDNA variation measured in single blood-forming cells, muscle fibers, eggs, tiny tumor samples, and degraded clinical specimens. At such tiny scales, stray DNA from outside is notoriously hard to avoid.

External contamination threatens the analysis itself: foreign DNA can masquerade as real variation. A false variant in a medical specimen could mislead diagnosis or research conclusions. The authors press the field to treat contamination as a central problem, not a footnote. Tiny samples demand strict controls, and this study explains why.
plos-pone-0000781:
John H. Malone, Thomas H. Chrzanowski and Pawel Michalak examined why hybrid male frogs are sterile, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproductive isolation defines populations as unique biological species. Yet very little was known about the gene expression basis for that isolation: which genes, behaving differently, make hybrids fail. Powerful molecular tools finally let researchers identify candidate genes in the act.

Their hybrids come from crossing Xenopus laevis with Xenopus muelleri, two African clawed frogs. Male hybrids are sterile, a common pattern in animal crosses. Comparing gene expression in hybrids against parents can locate the misregulated genes. Each candidate is a clue to how new species seal themselves off.
plos-pone-0000881:
Ketki Verkhedkar, Karthik Raman, Nagasuma Chandra and co-authors compared reaction networks in the germs behind tuberculosis and leprosy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Scientists build many kinds of maps for living systems, from gene control maps to maps of chemical reactions. Each map gives a different view of how a cell runs.

Here the team built graphs from the metabolome, the full set of small chemicals in the cell, for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium leprae. Comparing the two may show where their chemistry is shared and where it parts. Those differences matter, since one germ causes TB and the other leprosy, two very different diseases.
plos-pone-0000981:
Stina Enqvist, Knut Sletten, Fred Stevens and colleagues traced what decides which tissues amyloid strikes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Amyloid is clumped protein deposited outside cells. About twenty-five proteins can form it, and the diseases range from Alzheimer's to type two diabetes. In AL amyloidosis, the clumps come from antibody light chains.

The team argue that both the germ line origin of the light chain and later somatic mutations shape which tissues get targeted. That would explain why patients with the same disease differ so much in which organs fail. A tissue logic could improve prognosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001081:
Heiko Vogel and co-authors set plant gene answers to specialist and generalist insects side by side, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plants guard their leaves with traits that are always on, and traits switched on by attack. A few hormone paths control the switched-on set.

The study plant is Boechera divaricarpa, a wild North American kin of the lab plant Arabidopsis. The team track gene use under feeding by specialists, which eat few plant kinds, and generalists, which eat many. Each pest may call for a different guard. A wild kin shows answers that lab strains, bred for ease, may have lost. The contrast guides thought on how to keep crops safe.
plos-pone-0001181:
Diarrhea, respiratory infection, and malaria cause much of the illness and death in sub-Saharan Africa, and their levels rise and fall over time. Daniel Medina and colleagues built forecasting methods for these diseases in Niono, Mali, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their challenge is that the time series are non-stationary, meaning the patterns themselves keep shifting.

Forecasting tools that assume steady patterns fail on such data. The authors set out to model the real behavior of the three disease series in one district. Better forecasts let clinics and health programs prepare staff and supplies before a surge arrives.
plos-pone-0001281:
Blood tests for ovarian cancer markers can be thrown off by how the blood was handled before testing. Jason Thorpe and colleagues quantified that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Biomarker studies compare serum protein levels between people with and without cancer, and efforts are usually made to standardize collection and storage.

The authors examined the effects of blood collection conditions on ovarian cancer serum markers. If handling differences mimic or mask disease differences, early detection studies can mislead. Their work tells researchers which pre-analytical steps matter most, practical knowledge for any biomarker program.
plos-pone-0001381:
Dafna Singer-Lahat, Dodo Chikvashvili, and Ilana Lotan published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how hormone cells release their cargo. Cells that make hormones let them out in a step called exocytosis. Ion channels in the cell wall help set the pace of that release. The team studied how one channel type works with a partner protein.

The authors show that the channel binds direct to the partner protein, and that this bond boosts release. Work done before had used added genes in rat cells. This study checks the pair as found in real cells. The finding adds a fresh route by which cells fine tune the flow of hormones and brain signals.
plos-pone-0001481:
M. Abid Hussain and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a stomach germ's protein and the immune reply. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, causes stomach swelling and ulcers and raises cancer risk. Many of its proteins had been flagged as harm factors. The team studied one enzyme of the germ in people with ulcers or stomach swelling.

They report that this enzyme can draw a strong antibody reply in such patients. A strong reply marks the protein as a lead for tests or shots. It may help labs tell who hosts the germ. It also adds to the map of how this germ provokes the stomach lining.
plos-pone-0001581:
Zoran Popmihajlov and Kendall Smith published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a self brake in T cells. A signal called IL-2 drives the growth of T cells picked by a germ cue. A second factor acts as a brake on that growth. The pair asked how the two are wired, since a sound brake keeps immune replies from running too far.

They found IL-2 itself turns on the brake factor after T cells fire. That forms a neat loop: the gas builds its own brake. Loops like this set the size and span of an immune reply. Faults in them may underlie ills where T cells attack the self.
plos-pone-0001681:
Linda M. Sanderson, Philip J. de Groot, Guido J. E. J. Hooiveld, and their co-authors set out a new way to study how dietary fat talks to genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Fats in food likely affect health by changing gene activity. Several gene switches, including SREBP-1c, NF-κB, and the PPAR family, respond to fatty acids. What stayed unclear was how much of the response each fat type drives.

Their answer is synthetic dietary triglycerides: fats built to exact designs, so each part can be varied alone. The full text explains the design, the feeding tests, and the gene activity readouts. Clean, controlled fats let nutrigenomics, the study of food-gene links, move past the mixed signals of natural diets.
plos-pone-0001781:
André F. A. Santos, Renan B. Lengruber, Esmeralda A. Soares, and their co-authors mapped neglected regions of the HIV genome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Drug resistance data cover the first 400 amino acids of HIV's reverse transcriptase well. The C-terminal domains of Pol, named thumb, connection, and RNase H, were poorly understood, including what antiretroviral treatment does to them.

The team characterized conservation patterns in the connection and RNase H domains and identified new mutations in patients treated with NRTI drugs. The full text gives the patient sequences and the mutation map. Resistance can hide in unmonitored regions, so widening the map helps labs keep drug tests accurate.
plos-pone-0001881:
Hui Li and co-authors traced a gene choice shaped by past selection in East Asia in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The genes in view make alcohol dehydrogenase, a set of enzymes that break down alcohol in the body. One form of a gene in this set, known as ADH1B*47His, had been tied to a lower risk linked with drink.

The team studied how this form is spread across groups in East Asia and weighed signs that nature favored it there. Work like this tests how diet, drink, and local habits in the past can leave marks on genes today. It also helps explain why groups can react to alcohol in unlike ways.
plos-pone-0001981:
Deborah Tribouillard-Tanvier and co-authors found that a blood pressure drug fights prions, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Prion diseases are fatal, spreadable brain disorders with no cure, in animals and humans alike. Any drug already used in people that slows prions would be a fast lead.

The drug is guanabenz, long used for high blood pressure. As the title states, it was active in living animals against both yeast prions and mammal prions. Yeast may seem a far cry from brain disease, but their prions share core traits. A known, safe drug with anti-prion power is a rare and useful find.
plos-pone-0002081:
Abdisalan Noor and co-authors measured whether mosquito net use matches lower malaria in rural Somalia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Across Africa, efforts and funding to scale up insecticide-treated nets had grown fast over five years. Yet little was known about how well the nets work in south central Somalia, a hard region for health work.

The team surveyed net use and tested for infection with Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, in rural communities. Local proof matters, since net habits, housing, and mosquito behavior vary by place. The study gives Somalia's malaria program data of its own.
plos-pone-0002181:
Ahmedin Jemal, Elizabeth Ward, Robert Anderson, and co-authors measured the gap in death rates between rich and poor Americans, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. From 1960 to 1990 that gap had widened, mostly because heart disease deaths fell more slowly among poorer groups than among richer ones. No study had checked the trend with data past that period.

The team examined death rates from 1993 to 2001 across socioeconomic groups. They report that inequalities in death rates from all causes kept widening in those years. Numbers like these shape health policy, since they show progress in survival is not shared evenly across the country.
plos-pone-0002281:
Gareth Weedall, Spencer Polley, and David Conway compared rates of protein change across malaria parasite species, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparing genomes across the Plasmodium genus can reveal which genes are under strong natural selection. A bottleneck was data: only partial, low-coverage genome sequence existed for the closest relative of the main human parasite, Plasmodium falciparum.

The team asked whether genes flagged for fast non-synonymous change, changes that alter the protein, in one species keep that signature in others. They found the signatures correlate poorly across the genus. The caution matters: selection signals in one malaria species do not transfer cleanly to its cousins.
plos-pone-0002381:
Li and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Jianxu Li, Hongbing Wu, Jing Hong, among others. Its subject is odorranalectin Is a Small Peptide Lectin with Potential for Drug Delivery and Targeting. Lectins are sugar-binding proteins that specifically recognize sugar complexes.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002481:
Bueti, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Domenica Bueti, Eelco V. van Dongen, Vincent Walsh, among others. Its subject is the Role of Superior Temporal Cortex in Auditory Timing. Recently, there has been upsurge of interest in the neural mechanisms of time perception.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002581:
Elemans and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Coen P. H. Elemans, Andrew F. Mead, Lawrence C. Rome, among others. Its subject is superfast Vocal Muscles Control Song Production in Songbirds. Birdsong is a widely used model for vocal learning and human speech, which exhibits high temporal and acoustic diversity.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002681:
In 2008, Thorsten Pauly and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Activity-Dependent shedding of the NMDA receptor glycine binding site by matrix metalloproteinase 3: a PUTATIVE mechanism of postsynaptic plasticity. Authorship is credited in the record to Thorsten Pauly and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Functional and structural alterations of clustered postsynaptic ligand gated ion channels in neuronal cells are thought to contribute to synaptic plasticity and memory formation. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002781:
In 2008, Miguel Gaspar and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about multiple functions for ORF75c in murid herpesvirus-4 infection. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Miguel Gaspar, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. All gamma-herpesviruses encode at least one homolog of the cellular enzyme formyl-glycineamide-phosphoribosyl-amidotransferase. A further point appears in the abstract. Murid herpesvirus-4 (MuHV-4) encodes 3 (ORFs 75a, 75b and 75c), suggesting that at least some copies have acquired new functions. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002881:
Anthony Kong, Véronique Calleja, Pierre Leboucher and colleagues studied drug resistance in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drugs that block the EGFR receptor often help only some patients, and EGFR levels alone do not predict who will respond. The role of the related receptor HER2 was their focus.

The team reports that HER2 can keep cancer growth going by switching on other HER receptors when EGFR is blocked. In the title's terms, HER2 function escapes EGFR inhibitors that way. The finding points drug makers toward blocking more than one receptor at once in such tumors.
plos-pone-0002981:
Mattia Zampieri, Nicola Soranzo, Daniele Bianchini and co-authors asked where gene co-expression patterns come from in 2008. Reverse engineering tries to infer gene networks from large sets of microarray data. Such networks are widely used to deduce, merge, and validate claimed physical interactions between genes.

The team tested the patterns found in E. coli and baker's yeast against what reverse engineering algorithms produce. Their question is whether co-expression reflects real regulation or artifacts of the methods. Published in PLOS ONE, the answer helps researchers judge how much trust inferred networks deserve. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003081:
Kerry Dwan, Douglas Altman, Juan Arnaiz and co-authors reviewed evidence on publication and outcome reporting bias in 2008. Growing use of meta-analysis in systematic reviews had highlighted biases arising during randomized trials. Study publication bias, where results decide whether a trial is published, threatens review validity.

The systematic review gathers empirical evidence on both publication bias and selective outcome reporting. Published in PLOS ONE, it is evidence about evidence: how much trust pooled results deserve. Trial registration and full reporting reforms rest on exactly this kind of audit. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003181:
Ran Taube, Quan Zhu, Chen Xu and colleagues describe a display platform based on lentiviruses in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Isolating human antibodies with current display tools can be limited by problems with protein expression, folding, and later modifications. The team describe a discovery platform that uses self-inactivating lentiviral vectors for surface display.

Their system shows human antibodies stably on the surface of human cells and virus particles. Readers get a method that keeps antibodies in a human cell setting, where folding is more natural. That could improve the search for antibodies for research and therapy.
plos-pone-0003281:
Ya-Chun Huang and Neal A. Hessler study social effects on reward neurons in songbirds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Synaptic transmission onto dopaminergic neurons of the mammalian ventral tegmental area can be potentiated by acute or chronic exposure to addictive drugs. Because rewarding behaviour such as social affiliation can activate the same neural circuitry as addictive drugs, the team asked whether social context does the same in birds.

Their title reports that social modulation during songbird courtship potentiates midbrain dopaminergic neurons. Readers see courtship change the reward system at the synapse level. The work links social experience to the same machinery involved in addiction.
plos-pone-0007381:
Nancy O. Duah, Helen A. Weiss, Annette Jepson, and colleagues used twins to study inherited control of malaria antibodies in 2009. Understanding how far genetics regulates acquired immunity to common infections is important. A classical twin study can estimate the heritable share of variation in measurable immune traits between pairs of twins.

The authors assess antibody isotype and subclass responses to Plasmodium falciparum antigens. Different antibody classes perform different defense jobs. They estimate heritability of those responses. Their PLOS ONE results show how much malaria immunity runs in families, which matters for vaccine design.
plos-pone-0007481:
Tamara Broderick and David MacKay published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on choosing items with only a single switch. Some users can produce just one reliable input: a button press, a blink, or a sip of air. Selection methods built for them are often slow and rigid. The same problem appears in mobile devices and in secure communication. The authors present a method meant to be both fast and flexible.

Their approach lets a user pick from many options using only that one repeated signal. Speed comes from how the options are organized and timed. Flexibility means the method adapts to different tasks and users. For people with severe motor impairments, faster selection means faster speech and writing. The paper is a design contribution to accessible computing, with uses beyond disability as well.
plos-pone-0007581:
Nidia Alvarez-Rueda, Marlène Biron, and Patrice Le Pape published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Leishmania mexicana, a parasite that invades human cells. Invasion is a complex meeting of parasite and host machinery. Signals fire in both cells during the encounter. Little was known about protein kinase C and its relatives in the parasite during that meeting. The team measured a PKC-like activity as contact begins.

The parasite's infectivity tracked with that kinase-like signal. When the parasite touches a host macrophage, the signal switches on. That timing marks it as part of the invasion machinery rather than background noise. A trigger this specific is a possible weak point. Leishmania causes disfiguring disease across the tropics, and new drug targets are scarce. The study ties one measurable signal to the moment of entry.
plos-pone-0007681:
James Heron and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how the brain tells self-made events from outside ones. When we act, our actions produce sights and sounds. The brain must judge which events it caused and which came from the world.

The team used time shifts to study this judgment. People adapted to an artificial delay between an action and its effect, and their sense of timing changed. The shift worked across senses, not just one. That points to a shared timing system that sits above sight and touch alone.
plos-pone-0007781:
Amy Englert and Michael Greene published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how Brazilian free-tailed bats recognize their roostmates by smell. These bats are deeply social and crowd into roosts that can hold millions. Life in such crowds demands a way to tell friend from stranger.

The authors tested whether chemical cues guide both recognition and roost choice. Bats may use scent to find their own colony's roost among many. Chemical recognition in these vast colonies had barely been studied. The work adds smell to the story of how bat societies hold together.
plos-pone-0007881:
Ivo Ploemen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It makes the malaria parasite's liver stage visible in real time. After a mosquito bite, Plasmodium parasites first grow inside the liver. That phase is important, yet hard to study.

Infection rates in lab animals and cultured cells are low. The methods to watch parasites develop inside cells were also complicated. The team used real time imaging to visualize and count the rodent malaria liver stage. Clear numbers from this phase can speed vaccine and drug tests. The liver stage is a tempting bottleneck to attack.
plos-pone-0007981:
Maria Gonzalez and colleagues tracked plant virus particles meeting immune scout cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The particles come from cowpea mosaic virus, a plant germ now used as a carrier in vaccine design. To work, a carrier must first reach the cells that start an immune response.

Tests in dishes and in live animals showed how the scouts take the particles in and react. That meeting shapes how strong and what kind the later response will be. Knowing the details lets designers tune plant-virus carriers so vaccines built on them work better and safer.
plos-pone-0008081:
Edwin van Dellen and colleagues turned brain recordings into network maps in epilepsy patients for PLOS ONE in 2009. Temporal lobe epilepsy that resists drugs is often treated by surgery, usually after years of seizures. What those years do to local brain networks was little known.

Graph methods, which chart how points link, showed the networks around the seizure zone had changed their wiring over the long illness. The maps give surgeons and doctors a new way to read the cost of waiting. They may also help pick which patients gain most from surgery.
plos-pone-0008181:
Frank Norbert Gellerich and co-authors reported brain cell energy findings in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their work concerns mitochondria, the parts of cells that make most of the cell's energy. They studied how mitochondria in the brain respond to glutamate, a key signal chemical. The surprise lay outside the mitochondria themselves.

Calcium outside the mitochondria, at very low levels found in the body, switched on energy production. The effect was strong and worked only through this outside signal. It let mitochondria raise output on demand when glutamate was present. The finding changes how scientists picture energy control in brain cells.
plos-pone-0008281:
Andrew M. Prpich, Yuebiao Sheng, and Wei Wang asked a physics question in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Surface tension is a fundamental property of a liquid surface. It matters in natural, engineering, and biomedical processes. Research so far focused largely on the liquid side of a surface. Little attention went to the vapor side above it.

The authors asked which phase, liquid or vapor, matters more for surface tension. Their analysis reframes a classic concept in physical chemistry. The answer affects how scientists model droplets, bubbles, and films. It is a basic question with wide practical reach.
plos-pone-0008381:
Gerrit Volkmann and Xiang-Qin Liu presented a protein labeling method in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Site-specific labeling helps scientists study protein structure, folding, and interactions. Current methods for such labeling are few and limited. New methods are therefore needed by protein researchers. Their approach labels the tail end, the C-terminus, of a protein.

They combined a synthetic peptide with a split-intein to attach biotin. Biotin tags make proteins easy to pull out and track. Labeling only the tail end leaves the rest of the protein untouched. The method widens options for protein characterization.
plos-pone-0008481:
Helena Christiansen and co-authors study two collagen genes in zebrafish in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Collagens are strong proteins that shape tissues such as bone and cartilage. Most fibrillar collagens had been linked to human disease. Type XXVII collagen was a recent exception with no known role. The genes are called col27a1a and col27a1b in zebrafish. The team test what they do early in life.

They find both genes are needed to shape the notochord. The notochord is the early rod that guides spine growth. The genes also affect bone mineral buildup and later spine growth. Their loss thus disrupts the whole axial skeleton.
plos-pone-0008581:
Nathan Boles and co-authors study a checkpoint gene in blood formation in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Erythropoiesis is the process that makes red blood cells. It provides the body's oxygen transport system. It is highly regulated, yet few mechanisms behind it were known. Checkpoint Kinase 1, or Chk1, is best known for guarding DNA during cell division. The team test mice with only one working copy of Chk1.

Having half the normal dose causes anemia in those mice. Their red cell formation is defective as well. A DNA guard thus proves essential for making red cells. The finding links cell cycle control to a common blood disorder.
plos-pone-0008681:
Laetitia Chapel, Xavier Castelló, Claire Bernard, and colleagues used math to study dying languages. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article builds a simple model of two languages in direct rivalry. In the model, speakers drift toward the tongue they see as more useful or respected. Public action, like schooling or media support, can raise that standing.

The team tested two setups for how standing can change over time. They asked when a weaker language can hold on instead of vanishing. The model also shows how fast a language bounces back after a shock. Such work can guide real efforts to keep minority languages alive.
plos-pone-0008781:
Marla Keller, Pedro Mesquita, N. Merna Torres, and colleagues tested an HIV-blocking gel under real-life conditions. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gel, called PRO 2000, is a vaginal microbicide meant to stop HIV. Trials usually test such gels in women who abstain from sex. Sex itself can spread or dilute a gel, though. Semen can also blunt antiviral action in lab tests.

The team measured gel levels and antiviral strength after intercourse. Both the amount present and the killing power mattered for protection. Their findings shape how future microbicide trials should be designed. Real-world checks prevent false confidence from abstinent-only studies.
plos-pone-0008881:
Malathesha Ganachari, Jorge Ruiz-Morales, Juan Gomez de la Torre Pretell, and colleagues tested a two-gene combination for tuberculosis risk. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. One gene, MCP-1, helps call immune cells to infection sites. A variant form of it raised TB risk in unvaccinated Mexicans and Koreans. A second variant, in the MMP-1 gene, might add to that risk. Whether the pair matters in BCG-vaccinated people was unknown.

Vaccinated carriers of both variants developed pulmonary TB more often. The joint effect exceeded either variant acting alone. Gene pairs, not single genes, may decide many infection outcomes. The result refines genetic risk testing for TB.
plos-pone-0008981:
Victoria Abraira and co-authors tested whether two proteins that stick together in a dish matter inside the ear, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One protein, Lrig3, sits in cell membranes and shapes how tissues form. The other group, the ErbB receptors, relays growth signals into cells. Lrig3 is needed for the inner ear to develop its normal shape.

In lab tests the proteins did bind to each other. But animals suggested that this binding is not what builds the inner ear. The ear formed its shape through some other action of Lrig3. Publishing a clear negative result like this saves other labs a wrong turn.
plos-pone-0009081:
Vyacheslav Furtak and co-authors showed that disturbing one cell protein weakens HIV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Retroviruses such as HIV are obligate parasites that borrow host proteins to copy themselves. Host cells also hold proteins that restrict infection and defend them. Mov10 is part of P-bodies, the granules where cells store and process RNA.

Perturbing Mov10 sharply reduced HIV-1's infectivity in the team's tests. New virus particles still formed but were less able to infect fresh cells. The host factor thus helps the virus finish its life cycle properly. Blocking the help Mov10 gives is a possible new angle for antiviral drugs.
plos-pone-0009181:
Mariana Hecht and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns American trypanosomes, the parasites that cause Chagas disease. DNA can sometimes pass from one species into another and then be handed down to offspring. Such transfers are major events in evolution, but proving one happened is hard.

The team adapted a sensitive DNA test to hunt for parasite sequences inside human DNA. They looked for cases where trypanosome DNA had entered human cells and then passed to the next generation. Documenting that inheritance would show the transfer is not a one-off accident. It would mean parasite genes can become a lasting part of a human family line.
plos-pone-0009281:
Xiaoling Gao and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis remains a global health problem, and the BCG vaccine protects only unevenly. A kind of T cell defense, called type-1 immunity, is known to be vital for fighting the infection. Less clear was how different dendritic cell groups shape the fight.

The team took dendritic cells from mice infected with BCG, the vaccine strain. One subset, the CD8-positive cells, calmed the harmful reactions caused by a later challenge infection. The CD8-negative subset did not. That split suggests future vaccines should aim to engage the right dendritic cell subset, not just any immune response.
plos-pone-0009381:
John Tregoning and co-authors published this lung infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a major cause of lung illness in infants. CD8 T cells help clear the virus from the lungs. Too much T cell activity, though, causes part of the disease itself.

The team studied a chemical signal called MIP1 alpha, also known as CCL3. In mice, this chemokine set the balance between T cell groups in the lung. That balance decided how severe the illness became during a first infection. Tuning one signal might one day let doctors keep the cure while cutting the harm.
plos-pone-0011381:
Gregory Schimizzi, Joshua Currie, and Stephen Rogers reported in 2010 that the amount of one cell enzyme changes how well common cancer drugs work. The drugs attack microtubules, the rods that cells use to divide, and tumors often resist them. The enzyme, a kinesin that takes microtubules apart, varies in amount from cell to cell.

Cells making more of the dismantling enzyme responded differently to microtubule drugs than cells making less of it. That link means a simple measurement of enzyme level could help predict which tumors a drug will hit hard. Oncologists need such predictors, since the same drug can shrink one tumor and barely touch another. The study turns a basic fact about cell structure into a practical clue for matching patients to treatment.
plos-pone-0011481:
Franziska Meier-Stiegen and co-authors showed in 2010 that the same master signal switches on different genes depending on the cell it reaches. Notch1 signaling tells embryonic cells which identity to adopt, and it is reused across many tissues. If the signal is constant, the variety of outcomes must come from the receiving cells, and the team tested that idea during early cell differentiation.

The genes Notch1 activated varied with cellular context, and the targets included both drivers of cell lineages and inhibitors that restrain them. Turning on a driver and its brake together is a way to keep development precise and reversible. The context lesson complicates any simple story in which one signal means one thing. Drug developers who target Notch must reckon with the tissue they are in, since the same drug can push different programs in different cells.
plos-pone-0011581:
Juliette Pavie and co-authors compared five rapid HIV tests in a real hospital clinic, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health officials in several countries were urging wider HIV testing at the time. Rapid tests licensed in Europe promised fast answers, but their accuracy on mouth fluid versus finger-stick blood was still unclear.

The team ran the five tests side by side on both sample types in routine care, rather than in a lab alone. Their comparison shows how sensitivity shifts with the sample used. For clinics choosing a kit, the results give practical guidance on which tests and samples can be trusted.
plos-pone-0011681:
Lin Chen and co-authors mapped insecticide resistance in Chinese mosquitoes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pyrethroid sprays are used heavily in China and worldwide to control disease-carrying pests. The mosquito Culex pipiens pallens has increasingly survived those sprays through a change known as knockdown resistance, tied to its sodium channel gene.

The team examined variation in that gene across mosquito populations. Their molecular survey shows how resistance is structured and spreading. Accurate monitoring like this lets control programmes choose sprays wisely and slow the loss of their main chemical weapon.
plos-pone-0011781:
James Fordyce offered a caution about a popular evolution statistic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Family trees are increasingly used to infer how the pace of species formation changed through history. A common test compares observed branching times against a steady pure-birth expectation, using a measure known as the gamma statistic.

Fordyce shows a falling diversification rate does not necessarily signal an early burst of speciation. The same pattern can arise in other ways, so the standard reading overreaches. His interpretation guide keeps family-tree readers honest about what branches can and cannot say.
plos-pone-0011881:
Jean-François Pessiot and colleagues built in 2010 a software system called PeakRegressor for finding where a gene switch protein binds DNA. The switch in question is STAT1, which turns genes on during immune signaling. Knowing its true binding sites from sequence patterns alone is a standing puzzle in bioinformatics.

PeakRegressor combines motif pattern, position, and combinations of signals to pick out composite patterns that mark real binding sites. It also flags DNA variants that might disturb those sites and change gene control. Tools that read binding rules more accurately help explain why some harmless-looking DNA differences alter immune responses.
plos-pone-0011981:
Amandine Bemmo and co-workers profiled in 2010 how mouse breast tumors edit their gene messages as they gain the power to spread. Breast cancer kills mainly through metastasis, and changes in mRNA splicing, the editing of gene messages, are increasingly tied to cancer traits. The team compared tumors with different metastatic abilities at the level of individual exons.

The profiling revealed splicing changes specific to the more metastatic tumors. Each changed message can produce a protein version better suited to travel and colonization. A catalog of those edits gives researchers candidate switches behind spread, and candidate markers for judging how dangerous a tumor is likely to become.
plos-pone-0012081:
Marit Farenhorst and co-workers found in 2010 that a bug-killing fungus and a tired spray drug kill far more jointly than each does on its own. The spray, permethrin, is a main tool against the mosquitoes that spread malaria in West Africa, but the local kind can now shrug the drug off. Fungi that sicken and kill bugs are a known extra arm, long used on farm pests.

Put to the test on drug-proof mosquitoes, the fungus and the spray showed a true team effect: each made the other bite harder. That kind of team play can bring a cheap spray back from the dead, since the dose that fails alone may kill when a fungus has first sickened the bug. A fungus spray for house walls could thus stretch the life of the sprays malaria work now leans on.
plos-pone-0012181:
Zhengsheng Li, Megan Mulligan, Xusheng Wang, and co-authors traced wide differences between mouse strains to one gene change, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene makes COMT, an enzyme that clears dopamine and related messengers, shaping mood, thinking, and responses to drugs. A jumping piece of DNA landed in this gene in some mouse lines, changing how its message is built.

That one insertion explained broad differences in the enzyme's levels across the body and in behavior between strains. Studies using these mice to model human thinking or drug response must reckon with it. More broadly, the case shows how a single hidden variant can quietly drive many results blamed on other causes.
plos-pone-0012281:
Kwesi Frimpong-Boateng, Nico van Rooijen, and Ralf Geiben-Lynn studied how regulatory T cells blunt DNA vaccines in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses, a vital service against self-attack, but they may also muffle the first response to a vaccine and weaken it. Natural killer cells are among the earliest responders after vaccination, before the targeted defense assembles.

The team found the regulators suppress those early killer cells during plasmid DNA vaccination, weakening the later CD8 T cell response through a calming cytokine. If a vaccine's own brakes can be eased briefly, the same dose might protect better. That insight feeds the design of DNA vaccines, a platform long praised for safety but dogged by weak responses.
plos-pone-0012381:
Izabela Nowak, Edyta Majorczyk, Andrzej Wiśniewski and colleagues examined a natural killer cell gene in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The gene, KIR2DS5, switches on killer cells of the immune system, though its exact target is unknown. It had been linked to outcomes after stem cell transplants, prompting the team to test its ties to several human diseases.

They compared how often the gene appears in patients and in healthy people across those diseases. The pattern suggests the gene may guard against some conditions while playing no role in others. Such clues help explain why immune gene mixes differ between populations, and they point to diseases where killer cell activity deserves a closer look.
plos-pone-0012481:
Carl Drews and Weiqing Han modeled wind-driven water drops at the Gulf of Suez and the eastern Nile Delta, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Wind setdown is the fall in water level when strong wind pushes surface water away for many hours. The effect is famous from accounts of sea crossings in the region, and the physics can be tested with modern weather and ocean models.

The authors simulated sustained winds over the shallow waters and measured how far levels fell and exposed land appeared. Their results show setdown of real consequence under the right wind. Beyond the historical debate, the modeling informs coastal flood science, where wind-driven water moves both ways.
plos-pone-0012581:
Vanessa De Vooght, Jeroen Vanoirbeek, Katrien Luyts and colleagues showed that mouse strain choice can sway asthma model results, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Occupational asthma arises from workplace exposures meeting individual susceptibility. Their chemical-induced asthma model uses a workplace-like sensitizer, but labs use different mouse strains, and genetic background can quietly rewrite outcomes.

Running the model across strains produced different severities and immune patterns. A model whose answer depends on the strain demands careful reporting and strain-matched comparisons. The work helps occupational health researchers design studies whose conclusions survive the move from one lab's mice to human workers.
plos-pone-0012881:
Moore, Goetz, Van Doornik and co-authors tracked young trout on their first trip from river to sea. Coastal cutthroat trout and steelhead trout meet and hybridise in streams along the North American Pacific coast. What the hybrid young do at sea was largely unknown when they wrote in 2010.

Their study followed the early marine migration of wild cutthroat, steelhead and their hybrids. Different migration timing or routes change which fish survive and breed. That knowledge helps managers protect both parent species and understand the hybrids' place.  Tagging let the team follow individual young fish at sea.
pmc-10364581:
Members of the GBD 2021 Diabetes group report how diabetes spread across the world from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes now ranks among the top causes of death and disability on the planet. It harms people in every country, at every age, and in both sexes.

Using the newest data and methods from the Global Burden of Disease study, the team built estimates for each country and region. They also project how common diabetes may become by the year 2050. Health leaders use such counts to plan care, set budgets, and judge whether prevention work is paying off.
pmc-1552081:
Zamora, Abraira, Muriel, and co-authors introduce Meta-DiSc, software for pooling diagnostic test accuracy studies. Reviews that combine such studies increasingly guide doctors in practice. Yet at the time, no dedicated and complete program existed for this kind of pooling.

Meta-DiSc fills that gap for studies of how well a test spots disease. It lets reviewers gather sensitivity and related measures across many trials in one workflow. Better pooled estimates help clinicians choose tests with open eyes, knowing how often each misses cases or raises false alarms.  It remains a reference point whenever reviewers combine sensitivity results across studies.
pmc-5133381:
Burgess, Bowden, Fall, and their colleagues wrote in 2017 about sensitivity analyses for Mendelian randomization. Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants to test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. Studies increasingly use many variants at once, which raises the chance that some variants break the method's assumptions.

Sensitivity analyses are extra checks that ask whether a causal conclusion survives when those assumptions are relaxed. Different checks probe different kinds of violation, such as variants that act through other pathways. Robust causal inference matters because these results guide prevention and drug development. The paper supports analysts who must defend a causal claim built on genetic data.
pmc-5466781:
Tremblay, Aubert, Barnes, and their team led a consensus project in 2017 on sedentary behavior terms. Work on sitting and low-activity time had grown fast in health science. Growth brought a mess: fields used the same words in unlike ways, so studies were hard to compare.

The Sedentary Behavior Research Network ran a formal process to agree on clear terms and definitions. Experts from many fields took part, which made agreement hard but more valuable. Shared words let studies be pooled and guidelines be written in plain terms. The agreed set now anchors work on how long sitting time shapes the risk of chronic disease.
pmc-6300481:
Alessandro Cassini and colleagues estimated the burden of antibiotic-resistant infections in Europe in 2019. Drug-resistant bacteria threaten modern care, from surgery to cancer treatment. Counting the deaths and disability they cause is hard but vital.

Focusing on the European Union and nearby countries, the team modeled infections with key resistant bacteria. They estimate tens of thousands of deaths each year trace to these infections. Much of the burden falls on infants and older adults, and on hospitals. The numbers support stronger infection control and careful antibiotic use across the region.
pmc-6927181:
Christoph Hafemeister and Rahul Satija presented a normalization method for single-cell RNA data in 2019. Cells in such data vary in how many molecules get captured. That technical swing can masquerade as real biological difference.

Their framework models counts with a regularized negative binomial model and uses the residuals for analysis. This steadies variance across genes with very different average levels. Clustering and marker finding sharpen as a result. The method ships inside the widely used Seurat toolkit, so it reached thousands of labs quickly. The approach ships with clear guidance on when the model assumptions are likely to break down.
pmc-7234781:
Jonathan Rogers and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2020 on the mind and brain effects of severe coronavirus infections. They gathered studies from the earlier SARS outbreak, which began in 2002, and the MERS outbreak, which began in 2012. They then compared those older findings with early reports from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The review pulls together what doctors saw in patients during and after these infections, from confusion and agitation to longer lasting mood and thinking problems. By placing the new virus beside its two closest relatives, the authors give clinicians a grounded sense of which mental health problems to watch for. It remains a useful early map of a side of coronavirus illness that received less attention than lung damage.
pmc-7285581:
Li Yin and colleagues reviewed in 2020 the biology and treatment of triple-negative breast cancer, one of the hardest forms of the disease to treat. This subtype lacks three targets that guide therapy in other breast cancers: the estrogen receptor, the progesterone receptor, and a growth factor receptor called HER2. It tends to grow fast, spread early, and return after treatment.

The authors explain how this cancer is now split into smaller molecular subtypes, each with its own behavior and weak points. They then survey treatment progress, from chemotherapy backbones to newer targeted drugs and immune based approaches matched to those subtypes. For clinicians and patients, the review maps where real progress is being made against a cancer long short on options.
pmc-8265181:
Zhiqiang Pang and co-authors unveiled MetaboAnalyst 5.0 in 2021, a major update of a web platform for metabolomics, the study of the small molecules in a sample. Since its first release more than a decade earlier, the platform had become a standard way to analyze such data. The fifth version aims to close the gap between raw instrument readings and biological meaning.

The authors describe the new modules and workflows, which carry a dataset from processing through statistics to interpretation in one place. They also show example analyses that highlight the added power. By keeping the platform free and browser based, the team keeps advanced metabolite analysis open to labs without dedicated computing staff.
pmc-9184281:
Milot Mirdita and colleagues built ColabFold in 2022 to make protein structure prediction fast and open to everyone. Their tool combines the quick similarity search of MMseqs2 with the AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold prediction systems. The pairing makes the search step far faster and uses the prediction models more efficiently.

The authors report speeds that allow close to a thousand structures or complexes to be predicted in a day on modest hardware. Because ColabFold runs in a free browser notebook, a student with no computing cluster can fold a protein in minutes. That openness spread advanced structure prediction far beyond well funded labs, and the tool became a default in teaching and research alike.
plos-pone-0359881:
Natnapa Heebkaew Padchasuwan and colleagues built and checked a new survey in 2026 that measures how well university students in Thailand handle sexual health facts. The skill has a name: sexual health literacy. It means being able to find facts about sexual health, grasp them, and use them well. Thailand had no survey made for this task among its own students.

The team's tool is known by the short name SHL-US. They put it through the standard checks that show a survey is sound: that its questions hang together and that scores stay steady. A sound tool lets schools spot which students are left in the dark. It also shows whether health classes truly raise what students know.
plos-pone-0360081:
Mohsen Hesami, Mohammad Rahbari, and Ron Salzman studied in 2026 how maize plants change their gene activity after treatment with a natural biostimulant mixture. The mixture combines quillaja extract, from the bark of a South American tree, with fulvic acid, a substance from decomposed organic matter. Biostimulants are sold to help crops grow and withstand stress without being fertilizers themselves.

The authors track the plant's transcriptional responses, which genes switch on or off, over time and in response to particular stimuli. A time resolved picture shows whether the mixture triggers a quick alarm, a lasting adjustment, or both. Such evidence helps separate biostimulants that genuinely prime the plant from those riding on marketing, a live question in farm supply.
plos-pone-0359981:
Yifan Gu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies cultural sustainability in Qing dynasty China, between 1644 and 1911. The lens is kinship networks, and the evidence is marriage strategies among literary lineages, families known for producing scholars and writers across generations.

The analysis is quantitative, counting and modeling how these families chose marriage partners. Marriages could spread a family's influence, guard its status, or keep literary culture alive through hard times. Historians of China and of family strategy gain a measured view of how elite culture reproduced itself for nearly three centuries.
plos-pone-0349981:
Ying Liu and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It builds a workflow that runs from forecast to dispatch for a natural gas transmission network covering a whole region, planned a day ahead. Two parts anchor the workflow: station-level load prediction, forecasting gas demand at each station, and linepack target setting, deciding how much gas to store inside the pipes themselves.

Linepack is the network's built-in buffer, so setting its target well lets operators meet demand swings without strain. Joining forecast to dispatch in one workflow turns prediction into daily operating decisions. Gas network operators facing winter peaks are the readers for a day-ahead routine of this kind.
plos-pone-0332281:
Ranna Kíssia Alves das Neves and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies people in Rio de Janeiro who were hospitalized again after catching COVID-19 a second time, between 2020 and 2022. The authors examine associations with vaccination status and with sociodemographic and clinical factors, who patients were and what conditions they carried.

Reinfections that land people back in hospital are the costly core of repeat COVID waves. actions-and-reactions-pg2381: Kipling's 1909 stories of actions and reactions: engineers, soldiers, and the empire's machinery. "The Power of the Dog" and its companions show his mature art. Strong, vivid, and very Kipling. Kipling's machinery age roars through these stories.
plos-pone-0345881:
Yuthara Subasinghe leads a team of six interviewing gig workers in Sri Lanka about what keeps them going, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fourteen workers earning through platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr described their skills and drives in depth. The authors were after the interplay between inner motivation, interest and autonomy, and outer motivation, pay and ratings, and how digital skill feeds both.

Digital skill turned out to be more than a technical asset: it acted as a psychological enabler, feeding feelings of autonomy, competence, and connection that power inner motivation. Inner and outer drivers sometimes reinforced each other and sometimes collided, producing distinct motivation profiles across workers. The resulting typology suggests platforms could design feedback and transparent metrics that support, rather than control, their workers. The authors note the Sri Lankan setting bounds how far the lessons travel.
plos-pone-0358781:
Kimbley Asaso Omwodo leads a team of five testing whether low vitamin D tracks with preeclampsia in Kenyan mothers, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The dangerous blood pressure disorder causes about a fifth of direct maternal deaths in Kenya, and African data on the vitamin link are scarce. At a major referral hospital, the team matched fifty-nine women with the condition to fifty-nine without, pairing them by age, pregnancy stage, and number of previous births.

Blood vitamin D ran significantly lower in the preeclampsia group. Levels classed as suboptimal appeared in about a third of cases but in fewer than one in fourteen controls. Adjusted analysis confirmed higher odds of the condition among women with low levels. The study cannot prove the vitamin shortfall helps cause the disorder, but it strengthens the case for testing whether screening or supplementation in African pregnancies would prevent cases.
plos-pone-0351281:
Kholoud Saad Al-Saleh tackles a search problem created by the Arabic language itself, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Encrypted search systems let users query data without exposing it to the server. But Arabic builds dozens of word forms from one root. That bloats the encrypted index and hides matching documents behind spelling variants. The study compares four text preprocessing strategies, three stemmers and analyzers plus a segmenter, against plain normalization inside a working encrypted search scheme.

On a news corpus with benchmark queries, stemming shrank the vocabulary by up to eighty-three percent, with matching savings in index size and transfer cost. A surprise emerged on speed: the plain baseline answered fastest precisely because it retrieved the fewest documents, while better preprocessing found more and paid in time. Scaling tests reached tens of thousands of documents. The result is the first evidence based guide for choosing an Arabic preprocessor.
plos-pone-0355381:
Hanan Ibrahim Alsharif led a team of eight authors testing a wild plant against stomach ulcers in animals, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Alcohol can injure the stomach lining and cause ulcers. The team gave an extract of Tragopogon coelesyriacus, a plant with traditional uses, in a live animal model of that injury.

Alsharif's group found the extract reduced the ulcer damage. They linked the effect to calmer oxidative stress, less inflammation, and less cell death in the stomach lining. A plant lead like this needs much more testing before human use. Still, it marks a candidate rooted in traditional knowledge that drug researchers can now examine with care.
plos-pone-0353681:
Sudhir Venkatesan led a team of eight authors fixing gaps in virus surveillance data, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Counts of respiratory infections arrive as time series with missing stretches, from reporting delays or testing changes. Yet officials need cumulative totals to judge the size of a wave while it is still moving.

Venkatesan's team developed methods to estimate those totals honestly from partial data, showing uncertainty instead of hiding it. Honest estimates let planners act without pretending the record is complete. The methods suit any disease reporting system with patchy data, which is most of them during a crisis. Better gap-filling also improves later research that compares waves across years and countries.
plos-pone-0358481:
Orsolya Csötönyi led a team of eight authors testing a painless way to read pig gut movement, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Stress changes how the gut moves, in pigs as in people, but measuring that usually needs invasive tools. The team tested surface electromyography, which reads electrical signals from the skin surface.

Csötönyi's method detects stress-induced changes in gut motility without surgery or swallowed devices. A painless, continuous window into the stressed gut helps researchers study welfare and feeding with less harm to the animals. Pig studies also inform human gut research, since the systems are alike. Farm science gains a tool that can run during normal housing, not only in a lab.
plos-pone-0357381:
Fatemeh Gholamali Nezhad and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a pilot trial of an unusual depression treatment: gentle electrical stimulation of the face muscles. Standard treatments fail about a third of people with major depression, so new mechanisms are needed. The idea grows from the notion that activating expression muscles can shift mood from the body upward. Earlier feasibility work suggested practicality, and this registered trial tests it properly.

Sixty participants will receive twenty sessions over four weeks, half with real stimulation and half with a sham version, with neither patients nor assessors told who got which. The trial tracks depressive symptoms, anxiety, quality of life, and sleep, plus dropouts and side effects as measures of tolerability and safety. As a pilot, its real product is design knowledge: effect sizes and practical lessons to shape a large multisite trial.
plos-pone-0357181:
Shreya Battu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how COVID-19 treated immunocompromised patients in intensive care as the pandemic changed. Reviewing nearly eight hundred Stanford ICU patients from 2020 to 2022, they split the timeline into pre-Delta, Delta, and Omicron periods and compared survival between immune-weakened patients and the rest.

Across the whole period, immunocompromised patients died more. But the gap reached significance only in the Omicron period, when their ninety-day mortality ran far above the comparison group's. They also made up a growing share of ICU admissions by then. The authors argue the pattern may reflect Omicron-era realities: vaccines and treatments helped the general population more, while the immunocompromised stayed exposed as precautions lifted. Protection strategies, they argue, should be timed to who remains at risk, not declared over for everyone at once.
plos-pone-0356181:
Maia M. Sobejana and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for the Care for Muscle study, on exercise for people whose muscles are weak from rheumatic disease or age-related muscle loss. Endurance training is thought to feed the muscle's energy factories, while strength training builds the contractile machinery, but patients may respond differently depending on what is wrong inside their muscles. The trial randomizes just under seventy patients with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or sarcopenia to strength or endurance programs.

Training runs eight weeks, supervised sessions on cable and fitness equipment plus a weekly home session. The main outcome is peak muscle strength on a dynamometer, with ultrasound imaging of thigh muscle, biopsy-based measurement of mitochondrial function, blood inflammation markers, and walking endurance as supporting measures. By matching muscle biology to exercise response, rehabilitation might move toward schedules prescribed by disease mechanism rather than habit.
plos-pone-0357581:
Zelalem Addis and coauthors published a 2026 agronomy study in PLOS ONE on feeding hot pepper, a cornerstone of Ethiopian cooking, in the Amhara Region. Yields lag because soils are tired and losing organic matter. Over two seasons, six feeding regimes mixing liquid bio-slurry, a farm waste product, with standard nitrogen fertilizer in different proportions were compared, measuring soil chemistry and pepper yield in replicated plots.

Blends beat the extremes. Halves of each, and a quarter slurry with three quarters fertilizer, improved soil nutrients and produced the highest yields, above the unfed control, while returning the best profit per investment. The half-and-half blend is the headline recommendation for farmers with enough slurry, the quarter blend suiting those short on it. Farm waste, the study argues, can substitute for a large share of purchased fertilizer without sacrificing the harvest.
plos-pone-0357281:
Zhonghui Zhu and colleagues probe whether the sympathetic nerves that support the aorta also protect it from tearing. A tear in the aorta's wall is deadly, and nerve signals help keep the vessel healthy, but their role in early disease was unclear. In mice given a chemical that weakens the aorta, nerve activity markers rose early and tracked with breakdown of the wall's elastic layers.

Removing a nerve hub in the neck did nothing on its own, yet it sharply worsened tearing once the weakening treatment began, raising ruptures and spreading damage. Muscle cells in the wall also showed signs of shifting type after the removal. Zhu and colleagues conclude that intact sympathetic support guards the aorta, and losing it early can hasten disaster.
plos-pone-0355981:
Ashley Shanahan, Gwenyth Eichfeld, Levi Todd, and Anzela Niraula charted how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, behave across the stages of a standard laboratory model of multiple sclerosis-like damage. Their 2026 study fed mice a toxin that strips myelin from nerve fibers, then examined the brain's main white matter tract during early damage, peak damage, and early repair.

Microglia multiplied within a week and shifted into debris-clearing mode, eating damaged myelin while dialing down inflammatory signals, a profile tied to two genes involved in cleanup. In the retina, which has no myelin, the toxin still changed microglia directly, proving some effects bypass demyelination entirely. The timeline helps researchers separate helpful cleanup from harmful inflammation when testing therapies.
plos-pone-0356781:
Yan Jiang and colleagues report a surprising amplifier of bacterial toxin damage in the mouse brain: albumin. Albumin is the commonest protein in blood. Their 2026 study injected mice with bacterial lipopolysaccharide. This molecule triggers fierce inflammation. Some mice got the toxin alone, and some got it pre-mixed with bovine albumin. The team then examined brain blood vessels and barrier leakage. It also examined a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis.

At the lower toxin dose, the albumin mixture leaked more tracer into brain tissue. It injured more vessel cells. It raised more death and inflammation markers than toxin alone. At a high dose the advantage vanished, swamped by the toxin itself. Tests confirmed albumin physically carries the toxin into the brain. That mechanism may matter whenever infection meets a leaky barrier.
plos-pone-0356381:
Renato Luque-Benavides and colleagues reviewed eighteen years of patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising around the eye at a Peruvian referral center, the largest such account from a Hispanic-Latino population. Their 2026 retrospective study covered ninety-eight patients treated between 2000 and 2017 and followed for a median of two decades, relating tumor type, stage, and treatment to survival.

The orbit was the commonest site, and slow-growing marginal zone lymphoma made up half the cases. Slow forms did very well, with roughly nineteen of twenty patients alive at five years, while aggressive forms lost far more ground. Older age independently worsened outlook in the slow group. The long follow-up gives Latin American eye cancer care a rare local benchmark.
plos-pone-0356281:
Maheen Sughra, Aisha Irum, Muhammad Ibrahim, and Adnan Ahmad Khan re-tested a classic theory of health behavior against Pakistan's national survey. The survey covered more than fourteen thousand married women. The question was what really drives contraceptive use. Their 2026 study extended the Health Belief Model with fertility preferences and contact with the health system. It estimated the whole structure statistically across three nested versions.

Beliefs mattered, but modestly. Feeling threatened by pregnancy risks and seeing benefits in contraception each nudged use upward slightly. Contact with family planning providers mattered consistently. Fertility desires dominated everything, especially the wish to space births. The authors conclude programs in Pakistan should work through fertility goals and provider contact first. Belief campaigns are supporting players.
plos-pone-0356881:
Takefumi Yoshida and colleagues surveyed 587 Japanese elementary school students about refusing school, testing whether two strengths, resilience and solution building, the habit of constructing next steps toward goals, soften the behavior. Their 2026 study used self-report questionnaires and modeled the pathways separately for boys and girls.

For boys, resilience calmed refusal directly and also indirectly, by strengthening solution building. For girls, resilience worked only through the indirect route: it built solution skills, which in turn eased refusal. Both paths ended at the same place, children with more of both strengths resisted school less intensely. The authors suggest support programs teach concrete solution building to everyone, since it carries the benefit for both sexes.
plos-pone-0356481:
Joseph Harrison and Matthew Wallace estimate how long immigrants live, and how long they live free of disability, across England and Wales in this 2026 study. Using whole-population death records and three censuses, they built life tables for people born in thirty-seven different countries, measuring outcomes from age fifty. The aim was to test the popular idea of a healthy immigrant effect against both lifespan and healthy lifespan together.

Most migrant groups did outlive the England and Wales-born population and stayed disability-free longer. But several large groups broke the pattern: people born in Scotland and Ireland, and men born in Poland and Lithuania, had shorter lives and fewer healthy years.
