Women born in Pakistan and Bangladesh lived longer yet carried more disability. The authors stress that migrants are far from one group, and some need targeted public health attention.
plos-pone-0355481:
Khushbu Mishra and co-authors used national survey data from Nepal to test whether mothers' paid work improves young children's nutrition. Child undernutrition traps families in poverty across generations, so any lever matters. Their 2026 study applied matching and instrumental-variable methods to growth measures for children under five.

Maternal employment showed no statistically reliable effect on height, weight, or related growth scores. The authors explain that most mothers' work is informal, so income gains are small. Extra work also cuts time for feeding and care. Limited control by women over household money may further weaken the link. Mishra and colleagues caution against assuming mothers' jobs alone will fix child nutrition.
plos-pone-0355781:
Johannes Meyer zu Drewer and colleagues puzzled over extra hydrogen appearing in charcoal made with crushed rock. Such rock-enhanced biochar aims to store carbon twice over, by charring biomass and by letting minerals weather. Their 2026 study cooked wood with a silicate rock at two temperatures and many rock shares, then probed the products with advanced instruments.

Most mixtures barely changed carbon yield or char structure. One extreme batch, nearly all rock and cooked hottest, held far more hydrogen than expected. The team traces the surplus to three sources: hydrogen inside the rock itself, hydrogen clinging to mineral surfaces, and a pyrogenic coating over rock grains. The finding refines how such chars should be measured and credited.
plos-pone-0354981:
Rudrajit Majumder and co-authors hunted for existing drugs that ultrasound could turn into weapons against glioblastoma. This brain tumour resists treatment partly because the blood-brain barrier blocks medicines. Sound-activated therapy can strike deep tissue without surgery, but proven activator drugs are scarce. Their 2026 pipeline pairs machine learning with printed tumour models.

A classifier trained without reliable negative examples scanned drug libraries for ultrasound-responsive candidates, including drugs first developed for Alzheimer's disease and ovarian cancer. Promising picks were then tested in three-dimensional printed tumour balls that mimic the real tumour's oxygen-starved core. Majumder and colleagues present the combined screen as a faster route to repurposed brain tumour treatments.
plos-pone-0355681:
Megumi Sato and colleagues examine in 2026 how baker's yeast turns a gene called YGP1 on and off as sugar runs low or stays plentiful. The gene makes a protein sent out of the cell and rises when food is scarce. Cell cycle timing and stress responses both come into play in the control system the team mapped.

When sugar was plentiful, a binding protein kept the gene active in a rhythm tied to cell division, partly through a second activator. When sugar ran out, two stress factors switched the gene on strongly. The plentiful sugar route also helped cells handle acid and live longer.
plos-pone-0355181:
Murat Akın and Orhan Kahveci compare in 2026 blood levels of a compound linked to vessel health in people with sudden hearing loss in one ear and in healthy peers. Patients were seen at diagnosis and again weeks after treatment, with hearing tested by standard tone methods. The question was whether the compound helps explain the illness or predict recovery.

Levels were higher in patients at the start and stayed high after treatment, even as hearing improved. Higher levels did not predict who recovered, though they did help separate patients from healthy people. The authors read the compound as a risk marker rather than a guide to outcome.
plos-pone-0343481:
Yusuke Takatsuru and three colleagues published this 2026 brain-imaging study on how food preference shows up while people eat. Some older adults lose appetite partly because they struggle to picture foods they might enjoy. Using a light-based brain scanner that works at the table, the team recorded front-of-brain activity in healthy young adults.

Each volunteer looked at and then ate a standard home-style meal and a favorite dish they had bought themselves. Brain signals during eating differed by dish, and preference ratings tracked those signals. Takatsuru suggests the readings could one day help clinics judge appetite in older patients without bulky equipment.
plos-pone-0347081:
Alexander Cardaras led a team of eight authors on this 2026 paper about reading numbers out of bar charts in medical journals. Charts trapped as pictures inside PDF files block the large reviews that combine trial results. Their four-stage pipeline finds chart panels, reads labels, separates bars, and rebuilds the values from the axes.

Tested on eye disease trials against hand-checked values, the system recovered chart data with usable accuracy. Cardaras calls it a proof of concept: limited to bar charts and one field for now, but a step toward software that harvests published results at scale.
plos-pone-0355281:
Wei Sun and five colleagues published this 2026 pilot study of a possible warning marker for sudden worsenings of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Fifty people took part: patients mid-flare, patients stable, and healthy volunteers. The team measured how many neutrophil white blood cells carried a surface protein called PD-L1, alongside standard blood counts.

That neutrophil share ran higher in patients than in healthy people, and higher still during flares, where it also predicted flare status on its own. Sun calls the marker promising but insists larger multi-center studies must test it before clinical use.
plos-pone-0354681:
Gladys Estheysi Elías Solís and three colleagues published this 2026 review of gut-friendly supplements and childhood anemia. They gathered nineteen trials covering more than four thousand children, testing prebiotics, probiotics, and combined synbiotics against placebos or standard care, and rated how solid each result was.

Overall the supplements produced no meaningful gains in hemoglobin or iron stores, though one trial hinted probiotics might trim anemia rates. No serious side effects appeared. Elías Solís calls for larger, better trials in high-risk children before these products are promoted for anemia.
plos-pone-0352681:
Sun and colleagues, in a 2026 simulation study, work on sealing coal fractures with particles made from captured carbon dioxide. Coal mines lose injected fluid through cracks, which wastes pressure meant to free gas. Their idea kills two birds: lock away the gas as a solid inside the coal, and use those solids as a temporary plug during fracturing.

The team built a computer model of coal pores and cracks from CT scans, and shaped the virtual particles from microscope images of the real solids. They then simulated fluid flow with particles plugging different spots under different injection settings. Plugging position changed the pressure built up inside the coal and how much fluid leaked away. From the runs, they fit formulas linking injection pressure, crack size, and plug position to pressure and leakage, with a very close fit. A lab setup was designed to check the simulation against real coal.
plos-pone-0332781:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, present a better way to measure the sludge blanket in sewage treatment tanks. Knowing how deep the settled sludge sits helps a plant run cleanly, but murky water confuses existing sound-based meters, which pick up noise and misread the boundary. The team tested their method at a Beijing treatment plant.

Their meter uses an array of sound sensors and hunts for the strongest echo of sound energy bouncing off the sludge surface. Filtering smooths stray spikes, and a peak-picking method separates the true signal from leftover noise. A fault check flags readings that stray too far. In plant tests, readings deviated from true values by a small margin and varied only slightly between repeats. The authors say the method holds up in turbid conditions where optical tools fail, offering plants a sturdier way to automate sludge control.
plos-pone-0353381:
Mohan and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build an online simulation to measure how emergency doctors triage injured patients. Guidelines say the most hurt should go to trauma centers, but practice varies, and bad triage costs lives. There was no cheap, trustworthy way to measure a doctor's triage judgment, so the team recreated a small hospital's emergency department online.

Forty-five doctors worked through about twenty cases each, in a few minutes per case. Their answers were consistent across similar cases. Doctors also rated the cases as realistic. A behavioral analysis split each doctor's performance into sharpness of judgment and personal threshold for acting. Among doctors who saw enough real severe injuries each year, in-game sharpness matched their real-world record moderately well. The authors offer the simulation as a scalable yardstick for a skill that decides where ambulances should go.
plos-pone-0353781:
Nik Zatul-Iffah Mohd Nabil and two co-authors check the first hurdle for a new dyslexia screening test aimed at secondary school students, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Older students with dyslexia often go unspotted because screening tools are built for young children. The team's twenty-eight-item test focuses on the thinking signs of dyslexia, and they asked whether its questions are clear and understandable.

Ten experts and ten students rated every item. Experts gave most items perfect clarity scores, and both groups' overall ratings beat the accepted benchmarks. A few items needed plainer wording. Passing this face-validity check clears the way for the harder statistical testing that must follow.
plos-pone-0354181:
Atsushi Mihara and seven colleagues test whether the order of two bone-building drugs changes how fractures heal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mouse study. Both drugs help bones grow, but through different machinery: one mimics a parathyroid hormone signal, the other blocks a protein that brakes bone formation. Mice with a surgically cut shin bone received one drug alone, or one drug for a week and then the other.

Starting with the blocking antibody and switching to the hormone gave denser healing tissue and stronger bones than the reverse order, at equal total exposure. Cartilage lingered longer in the hormone-first groups, a sign of slower progress. Sequence, not just drug choice, may matter in fracture care.
plos-pone-0352981:
Catherine Jeanne Marguerite Meyer and five colleagues ask what tells a promising oil palm relative when to flower, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Brazil. Acrocomia palms could supply sustainable oil without clearing rainforest, but their flowering rhythm was blamed on the rains on shaky evidence. Six family lines from across South America, grown side by side in a research collection, were watched through three flowering seasons.

Flowering ran strongly from September to January, in step across lines and years. Day length, not rainfall or temperature, tracked the timing best; weather only nudged the years slightly apart. For growers, a day-length clock means flowering can be predicted and pollination managed — one more step toward domesticating this wild palm.
plos-pone-0353881:
Freidouny and colleagues measured stretch inside a false-limb socket liner in a 2026 early study. How a liner stretches against the skin affects comfort and fit for people who wear a leg prosthesis. Computer models often predict that stretch, but their guesses are rarely checked against direct measures.

One volunteer with a below-knee limb wore the liner through two stepping tasks while cameras tracked a dotted pattern on its surface. Camera measures were then set beside model predictions for the same tasks. Matching the two would build trust in models used to shape sockets. Even as a small first test, it shows a practical way to check fit science against real movement.
plos-pone-0353481:
Peixoto and colleagues tested ways to use DNA prediction for a state-run soybean breeding effort in a 2026 study. Predicting yield and seed quality from DNA can cut field costs and speed new varieties. Trials at eight sites over two seasons supplied data on yield, protein, oil, and maturity for six prediction models.

A classic ridge model performed best overall in their tests. Training it on most of the population, chosen at random to keep variety wide, gave the steadiest predictions. A rank-based index also helped pick lines that raised yield and oil together. The guidance is practical: breeding teams can adopt DNA selection without exotic models or huge training sets.
plos-pone-0352881:
Santos-Lázaro and colleagues ran nationwide genetic surveillance of drug-resistant tuberculosis in Peru in a 2026 study. Peru carries the highest burden of multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis in the Americas. Tens of thousands of routine lab assay results from 2019 to 2022 were combined into genotype patterns for first- and second-line drug resistance.

Deeper sequencing of a chosen sample checked cases where resistance was only inferred. Mapping patterns by region shows where resistant strains cluster and spread. Surveillance at this scale helps health officials target testing and drug stocks. It also warns early when new resistance patterns emerge in a high-burden country.
plos-pone-0353181:
Zhang and colleagues searched blood cells for a shared gene signature of autism and irritable bowel syndrome in a 2026 study. The two conditions often occur together, and stress hormone signaling is a suspected bridge. Gene data from both patient groups were mined with enrichment, network, and learning methods.

Genes responding to stress hormones were disturbed in similar ways in both conditions. Single-cell data located which blood cell types carry the signal, and drug databases suggested compounds that might reverse it. A shared signature could explain gut-brain links and point to treatments that calm both sets of symptoms at once.
plos-pone-0352781:
Aloka Gnanasekara, Anuradha Jayakody, and Kasun Perera present this 2026 PLOS One survey study from Sri Lanka. It asks whether the state should adopt blockchain tools in its work. Senior IT directors answered a set survey. The authors read the answers through three classic lenses for adoption choices. The lenses cover the technology itself, the agency, and the world outside it.

All three lenses predicted intent to adopt. Trust in the tool mattered. So did fit with current systems, safety, and backing from top leaders. Funds on hand, rival pressure, and rules that support the move also mattered. Perceived edge over old tools did not matter. Neither did current IT stock or partner pressure. The authors turn the findings into a step-by-step adoption frame for Sri Lankan agencies.
plos-pone-0352581:
Ahmad Rabbani and four colleagues develop plant-based food packaging films in this 2026 materials study. Their base material is cellulose acetate, spun into fine fibres. Aloe vera gel and lemongrass oil are blended in for flexibility and antimicrobial promise. Eleven formulations were produced under a structured experimental design. Strength, stretch, and stiffness were measured for each.

Cellulose acetate content drove most of the behaviour. More of it raised strength and stiffness but cut stretch. Aloe gel acted as a natural softener, trading stiffness for flexibility. Lemongrass oil helped only at low levels. Paired with high levels of the other ingredients, it weakened the films. Response models mapped these trade-offs, and the films were sorted into performance classes. Such classification helps manufacturers pick a recipe that fits a product's needs without endless trial batches.
plos-pone-0350181:
Zoe Rand and colleagues charted forty years of killer whale sightings in Washington's Salish Sea, home to two very different kinds. Southern Resident whales eat fish and are endangered; Bigg's whales hunt marine mammals and answer to different pressures. Using detection records from nineteen seventy-eight to twenty twenty-two, the team modeled how each kind's presence changed across seasons and years.

The fish-eating Residents faded: their chance of being present fell steeply over the period, with the sharpest drop in summer, long their peak season. Bigg's whales moved the other way, rising from rare visitors to a likely presence. The opposite trends show the two groups cannot be managed as one, and they hint at deeper shifts in the food web that feeds the Residents.
plos-pone-0351081:
Filippos Sofos, Zoi Pana, and Dimitris Drikakis built a pneumonia detector for children's chest X-rays that shows its reasoning as one readable formula. Most image AI hides its logic inside huge networks, leaving doctors with a verdict they cannot inspect. Their approach evolves a compact equation from a handful of texture and shape measures taken from the X-ray, measures a radiologist can recognize, like entropy and solidity.

The formula sorted the main dataset with accuracy in the high eighties and held up on a filtered independent test set at just under eighty percent. It was also checked and retuned on a dataset from another source. With vastly fewer numbers inside than a deep network, the equation can be printed, debated, and audited, a different bargain for clinics weighing trust against raw accuracy.
plos-pone-0351881:
Md Al Saber and a large team designed a candidate vaccine against mpox, the virus behind the twenty twenty-two global outbreak, entirely by computer. They compared sixteen viral genomes to find shared parts, then picked pieces of the virus's surface and envelope proteins most likely to train the immune system. Software stitched the chosen pieces into a single multi-epitope construct and simulated how it should behave.

The design aims for breadth, covering the strains circulating since the outbreak rather than one isolate. Computer checks covered immune targeting, shape, and safety flags, the usual first screen before any laboratory work. Nothing here has touched a cell or an animal, and the authors present it as a blueprint. Its value is speed: if an outbreak strain shifts, this pipeline can draft a matching candidate in weeks.
plos-pone-0351181:
Liposarcoma, a cancer of fat tissue in limbs and the trunk, is treated mainly by surgery, yet kidney trouble and muscle loss may shape who survives. Julian Kylies and colleagues reviewed forty-seven adults treated with curative intent, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Kidney function, muscle amount, and belly fat were measured from scans at diagnosis and again about eleven months later, alongside everyday functioning scores. Declining kidney function traveled with worse muscle measures, fading function, and higher death rates. The authors argue these treatable problems deserve routine tracking in sarcoma care, since catching them early could protect both strength and survival.
plos-pone-0348881:
Safdar Abbas Kazmi and co-authors built a magnetic nanocomposite for cleaning dyed water with sunlight in 2026. Textile dyes resist breakdown, and a catalyst that works in visible light and can be fished out with a magnet afterwards is attractive.

Joining iron oxide with titanium oxide at the nanoscale improved charge separation, the step that usually wastes light energy. A tuned recipe removed most of a yellow reactive dye at neutral acidity, following predictable kinetics. Scavenger tests identified the active species doing the work. Machine learning helped predict performance. A recoverable catalyst answers the usual objection that nanopowders pollute while cleaning.
plos-pone-0335581:
Chloé Tavernier and co-authors compared bat activity in farm solar fields with nearby grasslands in 2026. Solar farms are spreading over farmland, bats are already under pressure, and whether panels displace bats was poorly known.

Detectors recorded calls at the edges of six solar fields and twelve control plots across the year. Every one of the seven species turned up less over solar fields, both in nights present and in calls recorded. Landscape features modified the pattern but never erased it. As solar fields multiply, the authors argue, monitoring bat numbers, not just activity at a moment, becomes essential.
plos-pone-0348581:
Nan Zhang and co-authors improved three dimensional object detection from vehicle LiDAR in 2026. Self driving cars read the world as point clouds, which are sparse and uneven, so grouping points into objects is error prone.

Their method first separates ground from objects with a cloth simulation filter, then clusters with a tree structure that adapts its settings. An upgraded point network reads features at several scales with skip links. On two public benchmarks it reached high segmentation accuracy with fast per frame times. The pairing of careful clustering with deep reading is the design's answer to messy real road data.
plos-pone-0346581:
Aziza S Al Adhoobi, Saud M Al Jufaili, and co-authors mapped where two small killifish can live in Oman's desert streams, now and under a warming climate. These fish survive in wadis, the seasonal watercourses of an arid land, and both species are found almost nowhere else. Their 2026 study combined climate mapping software, field checks at twelve stream sites, and an audit of protected areas.

The southern species depended on monsoon moisture and stayed tightly restricted, while its northern relative ranged wider on winter rains. Climate projections pointed to shrinking habitat, and barely any of the best habitat sat inside protected areas. Surprisingly, streams ideal for the killifish held fewer other species overall, and dissolved oxygen proved the single most important water quality factor. The authors call for targeted protection of the best remaining streams.
plos-pone-0348281:
George Agyei, Augustina Angelina Sylverken, and co-authors drew blood from nearly a thousand people in urban and rural Ghana to chart immunity to the coronavirus over time. Where people live can shape exposure and how long protection lasts. Their 2026 study sampled households across settings in 2023 and 2024, then retested a smaller group a year later for antibodies against two viral proteins and for virus-blocking power.

Past exposure proved equally common in city and countryside, at about forty-seven percent in each. Among those followed for a year, half carried both antibody types, showing combined traces of infection and vaccination. Paired antibody responses actually rose between visits, suggesting fresh boosting despite some fading. Nearly everyone tested had neutralizing antibodies. The authors see durable population immunity, maintained by ongoing exposure.
plos-pone-0349781:
Kennedy Dodam Konlan, Hellen Akosua Asante, and Cecilia Eliason interviewed sixteen women in Accra, Ghana, about living with high blood pressure after childbirth, a dangerous and understudied phase of the condition. Their 2026 study recruited women from a regional hospital's postnatal clinic and explored their experiences in depth, sorting the conversations into themes.

Women swung between hope of recovery and fear of complications. Many felt confident following treatment yet struggled with lifestyle changes and home monitoring. Support from spouses, family, and health workers helped, while social stigma hurt. The authors recommend that midwives and nurses actively counter stigma and coach self-management, since the women's own accounts show the condition is managed socially as much as medically.
plos-pone-0349381:
Yosué Vera and colleagues studied cancer patients who developed bloodstream infections at a referral hospital in Lima, Peru, asking how many died within a month and what raised the risk. They reviewed two hundred ninety-three patients treated between 2020 and 2024. Most had solid tumors, digestive cancers were the largest group, and most had active disease.

Nearly a third of patients died within twenty-eight days of the infection. The first antibiotics chosen matched the infecting germ in about four of five cases. Resistant bacteria are a growing problem in Peru, and this is among the first local studies to measure their toll in cancer care. The numbers give Peruvian oncologists a baseline for improving infection response.
plos-pone-0337381:
Diego Lievano Parra and colleagues used rats with partial damage to the brain's dopamine system to watch walking problems emerge over time, modeling the hidden early phase of Parkinson's disease. A low dose of a toxin was placed on one side of the movement center. For six weeks the rats crossed a horizontal ladder while camera software tracked every step and slip.

Stepping errors rose after the lesion, peaked around the third week, and then eased somewhat while staying above normal. Walking speed changed less consistently, and patterns differed somewhat between males and females. Because early Parkinson's is nearly impossible to catch in people, a timed map of the first motor slips in animals gives researchers a window for testing protective treatments.
plos-pone-0348681:
Hal Whitehead, Christine M K Clarke, and Ana Eguiguren report that sperm whales off the Galápagos Islands learned to relax around the research boats that photograph them. Photo identification is the backbone of whale science, but a wary whale ruins both the picture and the data. The team tracked how photographic quality and the distance whales allowed changed as individual whales accumulated encounters with the boats.

Experienced whales let boats come closer, and the share of poor, distant photographs fell, clear signs of habituation rather than growing stress. Tolerance made the research itself work better, yielding cleaner identification records. The authors recommend that any long-term wildlife study check for such learning, since animals that habituate, or the opposite, quietly change what the data mean and how ethical the disturbance is.
plos-pone-0349181:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 notice withdrawing an earlier mouse study claiming that a careful balance of dietary fats eased a disease model of a protein disorder. Readers should not rely on the original findings. The notice grew out of questions about a key figure and about how the animal work was reported.

Part of one figure panel looked much like part of another said to show a different group. The author blamed a preparation error and sent fixes, but editors found still more concerns in the new panels and data. Error bars in several figures also looked unreliable on review. Details about humane endpoints and euthanasia had been missing from the paper as well.
plos-pone-0348781:
Abel Jonathan Mussa and co-workers survey fungi in mountain soils in Tanzania that kill insects from within. These fungi help hold pest numbers down in nature, but their spread across tropical farm hills is barely mapped. Their 2026 study samples soils at three heights on the Uluguru slopes, in both farmed and fallow fields, and identifies fungi by DNA and by growing them.

Fourteen species turned up, led by two families known for insect killing. Farmed soils at middle and high levels held richer fungal life than fallow ones. In early lab tests, two species killed some fall armyworm caterpillars, a major crop pest. The survey gives farmers and scientists candidate fungi for gentler pest control.
plos-pone-0344581:
Hao Pei and co-workers simulate the noise of a large urban electricity substation and design a package of fixes. Transformer hum can disturb nearby homes and offices, and builders need to know what works before concrete is poured. Their 2026 study models one city substation with standard sound software and tests layout changes, barriers, silencers, and stronger enclosure walls in the model.

Barriers and smart layout cut the transformer's noise by a fair band of decibels. Bolt-on silencers took off a further chunk. Improved enclosure walls gave the biggest single cut, enough to bring emissions within safe limits in the simulation. The recipe gives engineers a worked example for quieting substations in noise-sensitive districts.
plos-pone-0347781:
Aleena Vikraman and colleagues study why lab-grown stem cells age, in this 2026 PLOS ONE cell biology paper. Stem cells taken from fat are prized for therapy, but under stress they senesce: they stop dividing and lose healing power, partly because their cleanup system for worn-out mitochondria falters.

Two familiar antioxidants, melatonin and coenzyme Q10, were tested for rescue. In stressed cells the pair restored the cleanup process and the upkeep of mitochondrial proteins, easing the senescent state and protecting the cells' ability to keep growing. If the effect holds up, simple antioxidant treatment could help laboratories keep therapeutic stem cells younger and more useful for longer.
plos-pone-0348081:
Eva Cappelli, Marianna Azzolini, and Cristina Ferrari studied nurses who face drug-resistant infections daily. Their study took place in two Italian intensive care units. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients with resistant germs demand strict hygiene steps. Emergencies push staff to cut corners at the same time.

The team watched care in action for months. They also held twenty-one interviews with nurses, aides, and doctors. Resilience worked at three levels, they found. Personal resources mattered, and so did team habits. Backing from the hospital mattered most of all. Nurses bent the rules with care rather than dropping them. The authors urge hospitals to build resilience into staffing and training.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Into the 1970s, the Cyprus force rolled on by six-month steps. On 9 June 1970, the Council adopted Resolution 281 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed to keep peace. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-June.

The text restates the whole Cyprus series back to 1964. It urges the parties to use the hopeful climate for joint work. It then extends the posting to 15 December 1970. The standing hope appears once more. Progress toward a final deal might by then let the force shrink or leave. That phrase had become the mission's refrain by 1970.

Part-heard war crimes trials in The Hague needed a rule fix in 2005. On 18 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1581 without dissent. The Yugoslavia court was racing to finish trials on a set schedule. Several stand-in judges sat on big cases as their terms ran out. Losing them mid-trial would waste years of work.

The text rules that named judges will finish the cases they began. The list covers five trials. Names include the Hadžihasanović, Orić, and Limaj cases. The Krajišnik and Halilović cases are there too. The fix spared the court from restarting long trials with fresh panels. It also guarded each accused person's right to a timely trial.

Croatia demanded a smaller, reshaped UN presence in 1995. The old protection force was being split into separate missions. Resolution 981, adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995, created UNCRO, the UN Confidence Restoration Operation in Croatia. It followed the Secretary-General's report of 22 March. Its mandate ran to 30 November 1995.

UNCRO would watch the 1994 ceasefire between Croatia and local Serb forces. It would track arms crossing from Bosnia and Yugoslavia. It would help aid reach Bosnia across Croatian land. It would also watch demilitarization on the Prevlaka peninsula. The Council even allowed air support to defend UNCRO staff. The hope was that confidence might grow into a negotiated settlement.

South Africa's race laws drew a world arms call in 1963. Thirty-two African states brought the case to the Council. Pretoria had jailed men for fighting its apartheid rule. It was piling up arms, some used to crush dissent. It had spurned a call to send a man to be heard. Resolution 181 passed on 7 August 1963 by nine votes to none. France and Britain held back.

Apartheid was damned as a breach of the Charter's word. South Africa had to drop its race laws at once. All held for fighting them had to walk free. Then came the sharp edge. All states were called, in grave terms, to halt arms sales to Pretoria at once. Guns, shells, and war trucks were named. Word on the scene was due from the chief by 30 October.

Resolution 381, adopted on 30 November 1975 by thirteen votes to none, renews the peacekeeping force stationed between Israel and Syria. The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force had watched the Golan separation lines since 1974. The Secretary-General's report on the force and his talks with all parties were before the Council, which voiced concern at continuing tension.

Three decisions follow. The Council set 12 January 1976 to resume debate on the Middle East, the Palestinian question included, in light of all past rulings. It renewed the observer force's mandate for another six months. And it asked the Secretary-General to keep it informed on further developments, the standard leash on a force renewed in short cycles.

Armed incidents strain Georgia's ceasefire in Resolution 1781, adopted in October 2007. A rocket-firing incident in the upper Kodori Valley on 11 March 2007 and a further incident on 20 September had been investigated by the Joint Fact-Finding Group. Trust between the Georgian and Abkhaz sides stayed low, and documents on the non-use of violence and on refugee return remained unfinished.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 15 April 2008. It calls for a stronger observation capacity for the mission and urges Georgia to bring the upper Kodori Valley in line with the 1994 Moscow Agreement, while the Abkhaz side shows restraint. Both sides must sign the two pending documents without delay, resume regular quadripartite meetings, and protect the right of all refugees and displaced persons to return, starting with the Gali region. It welcomes UNOMIG police deployment in Gali and urges deeper cooperation there.

A UN observer mission for Sierra Leone is created in Resolution 1181, adopted on 13 July 1998. The restored government was rebuilding under a disarmament plan agreed with international donors, ECOMOG provided security and ran arms collection, and rebel remnants kept attacking civilians.

The Council establishes the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, for six months until 13 January 1999, with up to 70 military observers and a small medical unit. UNOMSIL must monitor the security situation. It must watch the disarmament and demobilization of former combatants in secure areas and ECOMOG's role there. It must monitor respect for international humanitarian law. It must follow the Civil Defence Forces' voluntary disarmament. About 40 observers deploy first to ECOMOG-secured areas, the rest as security allows, once security arrangements and a status of mission agreement are confirmed. Its civilian staff advise on police reform and report human rights violations.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 181 (II), adopted on 29 November 1947, recommended the partition of Palestine. Britain planned to end its mandate by 1 August 1948. The Assembly, acting on its Special Committee's report, proposed the Plan of Partition with Economic Union. It proposed it as the way to settle the land's future government.

The plan called for separate Arab and Jewish states, joined in an economic union. Jerusalem was to be under a special world regime run for the United Nations. A five-state commission was to take over rule step by step and set borders. It was to set up temporary councils leading to elections and democratic constitutions, with equal rights for all.

Resolution 69/81, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, presses for entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. It notes that 183 states had signed and 163 had ratified. But only 36 of the 44 states whose ratification is required had done so. It urges those states to ratify without delay or conditions. It calls on all states to keep their test moratoriums while the verification regime is completed.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: On the Golan Heights, the force that watches the separation between Israeli and Syrian troops is renewed on 27 November 2001. UNDOF, the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force, stays in place for six months, until 31 May 2002. The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once, and asked for a report on developments at the end of the period.

What short-term judges may do at the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is widened on 19 May 2003. The tribunal's president had raised the point in letters. Ad litem judges were called in for a single trial, and their powers stopped there, even when other work sat waiting.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended article 13 quater of the tribunal's Statute. While appointed to a trial, an ad litem judge may now also handle pre-trial work in other cases, where the need arises and the judge is able to take it on. The replacement article is annexed. The small change aimed to speed the tribunal's crowded trial schedule.

Four months, with cuts, are granted to UNMEE on 31 May 2006. The Ethiopia-Eritrea mission is extended while being reshaped smaller. The parties had not met the Council's demands, and the border remained unmarked. The Temporary Security Zone between the two armies still had to be respected.

A reconfiguration of UNMEE's military component to a smaller size, matched to the stalled process, is authorized. Full compliance with resolution 1640 is demanded, including free access and support for the mission. Both parties are called on to cooperate fully with the Boundary Commission so demarcation can move forward. They are also to create the conditions for the commission's ruling to be carried out on the ground.

UNAMID, the joint African Union-United Nations mission in Darfur, is extended for twelve months on 30 July 2009, to 31 July 2010. The mission had taken over from the African Union force at the start of 2008. Violence against civilians, peacekeepers, and aid workers in Darfur continued, and no lasting ceasefire held.

All parties are demanded to end violence and attacks at once, meet their duties under human rights and humanitarian law, and commit to a sustained ceasefire. The Secretary-General is asked to develop a better ceasefire monitoring mechanism with the parties. UNAMID is told to report major violations and to use its full mandate to protect civilians across Darfur, while political talks toward a lasting settlement are pressed forward.

Civilians in the lands held by Israel were the subject of Resolution 681, adopted in December 1990. The Secretary-General had reported on ways to keep Palestinian civilians safe there. Israel had rejected Resolutions 672 and 673, which concerned a fact-finding mission. It had also decided to resume deportations of Palestinians. 

The Council expressed grave concern at Israel's rejection of the two resolutions. It deplored the renewed decision to deport Palestinians. Israel was urged to accept that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies in law to all the lands held since 1967. It had to obey that pact fully and carefully. The Secretary-General was asked to develop one idea from his report. The states that signed the pact might meet to discuss protection. With the Red Cross, he also had to watch the situation of civilians there and report every four months.

A short procedural decision from the early United Nations was taken on 24 May 1950. The Council had before it a note from the Secretary-General, dated 13 May 1949. The note concerned a General Assembly resolution of 28 April 1949. Resolution 81, adopted unanimously, does two things only. The Council took note of the Assembly's resolution. It then decided that, if a suitable occasion arose, it would base its own action on the principles set out in that text. That pledge is the whole content of the resolution.
un-sc-res-281:
Mid-1970 found the Cyprus peacekeeping force due for another term. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 June, said the force was still needed to maintain peace on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should continue beyond 15 June 1970. Resolution 281 was adopted unanimously on 9 June 1970.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They also had to make good use of the favorable climate and keep working together toward the Council's goals. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 December 1970. The text follows the settled form of these renewals, which kept the mission in place through years of slow diplomacy.
un-sc-res-1581:
Trials at the Yugoslavia war crimes court were running past the terms of the short-term judges hearing them in 2005. Six judges sat on cases that had not finished. The Secretary-General had asked the Council to act, in a letter dated 6 January 2005. The court's president had restated its plan to complete all work on schedule. Resolution 1581 was adopted unanimously on 18 January 2005.

The Council decided that the judges named in the text would stay on after their terms ended. Once replaced as short-term judges, they would keep serving until the trials they had begun were done. The cases included the Hadžihasanović, Orić, Limaj, Krajišnik, and Halilović trials. Letting a judge vanish mid-trial would have stalled those cases, or forced them to start again. The decision kept the trials moving, and it served the court's wider plan to finish its work on time.
un-sc-res-981:
Croatia gained its own United Nations operation in the spring of 1995. On 31 March 1995 the Security Council established UNCRO. The name means United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation. The Secretary-General's report of 22 March supplied the design. The mission would run until 30 November 1995. It replaced the Croatia part of the wider UNPROFOR force.

The Council restated its search for a negotiated end to the Yugoslav wars. It stressed respect for the borders of all states in the region. It also stressed mutual recognition among them. The Secretary-General had to keep consulting on the details of the mandate. He would report on the talks as the mission deployed. UNCRO's life proved short and stormy.
un-sc-res-181:
South Africa's apartheid system faced the Council in the summer of 1963. Thirty-two African states had brought the question forward. On 7 August 1963 the Council strongly condemned South Africa's racial policies. Apartheid, it said, clashed with the Charter and with South Africa's duties as a member. A special committee's reports had documented the system. World opinion, voiced in the General Assembly, ran the same way.

South Africa had to abandon apartheid and discrimination at once. It had to free everyone jailed or restricted for opposing those policies. All states were called on to stop selling arms to South Africa. Guns, ammunition, and military vehicles were covered. The Secretary-General had to report by 30 October 1963. The text began the long sanctions campaign against apartheid.
un-sc-res-381:
The Golan Heights observer force was renewed by the Security Council on 30 November 1975. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force and had talked with all parties about the Middle East. The Council voiced concern over the continued tension in the area. It also looked beyond the force to the wider Arab-Israeli dispute.

The Council renewed the observer force's mandate for six more months. It decided to reconvene on 12 January 1976 to continue the debate on the Middle East problem, including the Palestinian question. All relevant United Nations resolutions were to be taken into account at that session. The Secretary-General was asked to keep the Council informed of further developments. The pairing of a routine renewal with a set date for a broad debate shows the Council treating the Golan posting as one part of an unsettled regional question.
un-sc-res-1781:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1781, adopted in October 2007. Armed incidents had hurt the peace process, and some had cost lives. A rocket attack in the upper Kodori valley in March 2007 remained under joint investigation. Trust between the two sides stayed low.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 15 April 2008. It asks that the mission's watching capacity be strengthened. Both sides must finish papers on the non-use of violence and on refugee return without delay. Georgia must keep the Kodori valley in line with the 1994 Moscow cease-fire deal. Refugees keep their right to go home, starting with the Gali region.
un-sc-res-1181:
Sierra Leone drew a formal Council decision in Resolution 1181, adopted on 13 July 1998. The elected government had been restored with West African help. Former junta fighters and rebels still resisted and attacked civilians. A disarmament plan had been agreed with donors and now needed watching on the ground.

The Council creates the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, called UNOMSIL, for six months until 13 January 1999. Up to 70 military observers deploy, about 40 of them first to areas held by the West African force. They track security, watch disarmament camps, and check respect for humanitarian law. Civilian staff advise on police reform and report on human rights abuse.
europmc-pmc10266981:
Pang and co-authors argue that the physical shape of the brain strongly constrains how it works, in a 2023 study. The classic view holds that brain activity flows through networks of specialized cell groups wired together. Pang's team asks how much of that activity can be explained by the brain's geometry alone, through waves traveling across its folded surface.

They model brain activity as waves shaped by the cortex's form. The model matches observed activity across many tasks at least as well as wiring-based models. The study reframes how shape and function relate in the brain.
europmc-pmc10310781:
Zhang and co-authors published a 2023 review on drugs that target amyloid beta in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid beta is a small protein that builds up in clumps in the brain. Many scientists have blamed those clumps for driving the loss of memory and thinking in this illness.

The review traces the amyloid idea over 30 years of work. It notes that many trials of anti-amyloid drugs failed, which raised real doubt about the idea. It then notes that some recent trials did succeed. Zhang weighs open questions about current drugs and sets out ways to build better ones for care and for prevention.
europmc-pmc10364581:
The GBD 2021 Diabetes Collaborators measured the world burden of diabetes from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes is a long-term illness in which blood sugar runs too high. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also forecasts how common the disease will be through 2050.

In 2021, 529 million people lived with diabetes across the globe. The team split cases into type 1 and type 2 forms. Type 2 is the far more common form, tied to weight, diet, and low activity. The study weighed 16 risk factors for the type 2 burden. Lost healthy years were counted as deaths plus years lived with the illness. Forecasts used social and weight trends to project the rise.
europmc-pmc1054881:
Hauf and co-authors studied in 2005 how a protein ring lets go of chromosomes as cells divide. The ring, cohesin, holds twin copies of each chromosome side by side. At division, most of the ring leaves the arms of chromosomes early, well before the twins split. Two kinases, enzymes that add phosphate tags, drive that exit.

The team hunted tag sites on all four cohesin parts with a mass tool. Hauf found that tags on one part, Scc1, were not needed for the early exit. Tags on a second part, SA2, proved vital for it. Cells with a tag-proof SA2 kept cohesin stuck on the arms. The work pins SA2 as the key target of the kinase Plk1 in this path.
europmc-pmc10857981:
Xue and colleagues review a signal path that helps cancers spread in this 2024 paper. Spread, called metastasis, causes about nine in ten cancer deaths. One driver is a change called EMT, where anchored cells loosen and gain the power to move. The Wnt and beta-catenin path, a chain of signals inside cells, is a key switch for that change.

When the path switches on, beta-catenin builds up and moves into the cell nucleus, the control centre, where it turns on spread genes, the review says. This axis is overactive in many cancers of organs and blood. It also helps tumours resist drugs. Small RNA pieces and plant-based chemicals can damp the path in lab studies. The authors present the axis as a target worth aiming drugs at.
europmc-pmc11223881:
Bugnon and colleagues present the 2024 release of a free web docking service in this paper. Molecular docking predicts how a small drug molecule binds a protein target. It can speed drug screening by ranking candidates before lab tests. SwissDock, first released in 2011, prepares molecules and targets automatically for users.

The old docking engine was replaced by two state-of-the-art programs, the authors report. AutoDock Vina gives faster predictions, while Attracting Cavities gives more accurate ones. Molecules can be imported as files, as SMILES text strings, or as sketches drawn on screen. Targets come from uploaded files or a database ID. The interface was fully redesigned for interactive submission and analysis. Advanced search options link users to widely used databases for both molecules and targets.
europmc-pmc11226681:
O'Leary and a large team describe a US resource for fetching sequence data across the tree of life in this 2024 paper. NCBI Datasets is run by the National Center for Biotechnology Information. It gives simple, direct access to sequences, annotations, and metadata covering many species. Public repositories struggle to keep growing data discoverable and usable.

Data arrive as packages of sequences plus metadata, which aids sharing and reuse, the authors report. Access comes through web pages, command-line tools, and documented program interfaces. The resource follows the FAIR principles: data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The paper outlines the current scope of data on offer. It also explains the options for exploring and downloading packages. Proper delivery, they note, supports credit for data producers.
europmc-pmc11252281:
Liu, Zhou, Tan, Siu, and Guan survey the modern menu of cancer treatments in this 2024 review. Classic chemotherapy and radiation burden patients with heavy physical and mental strain. Care has since been transformed by more precise options. Small molecule targeted agents, antibody-drug conjugates, cell-based therapies, and gene therapy now lead the new wave.

Antibody-drug conjugates pair a homing antibody with a toxic payload. The review works through five classes: small molecule drugs, antibody drugs, peptide drugs, gene therapy, and cell therapy. For each it explains the method, development status, clinical challenges, and potential. These modalities target tumours personally and precisely, the authors say, and can improve patient comfort. Untapped headroom remains in all of them. The authors frame the comparison as a guide for both clinic and lab.
europmc-pmc1190181:
Shiffman and colleagues built a scoring tool for medical guidelines in 2005. Guidelines tell doctors what best care looks like. Many still fail to change daily practice. A guideline that is hard to apply will often sit unused.

Their tool, called GLIA, rates how easy a guideline is to use. It has 31 items grouped in ten areas. Clear wording, clear actions, and clear outcomes count as core areas. Shiffman tested the tool with expert review and trial use. Spotting barriers early can save costly failed rollouts. Clear actions are the Decide and Execute dimensions in GLIA.
europmc-pmc11926181:
Vogler and co-authors reviewed a protein family that controls cell death. The family is called BCL2, named after a blood cancer gene. Its members govern whether a cell releases a signal to self-destruct. That signal comes from mitochondria, the cell power stations.

Drugs that mimic natural blockers can free that death signal in cancer. Venetoclax, the first such drug, changed care for several blood cancers. Newer drugs and guided carriers are now in trials. Vogler also covers roles beyond cancer and newer drug designs. The review links basic cell biology to bedside use.
europmc-pmc1240281:
Meerts and co-authors tested flame retardant chemicals for hormone action in 2001. The chemicals, called PBDEs, are added to plastics and fabrics. They persist in nature and had turned up in human fat and blood. Their hormone effects were largely unknown.

Cell tests measured estrogen-like activity with a glowing reporter gene. Eleven PBDE types showed estrogen-like effects in breast cells. One altered form beat the natural hormone in strength, at far higher doses. Related bisphenol compounds varied with their bromine load. Meerts flags a hormone concern for this chemical family.
europmc-pmc1315281:
Stranger and co-authors mapped DNA variants that alter gene expression in humans in 2005. Medical genetics hunts variants behind complex traits. Reliable assays and maps are prerequisites for that hunt. The team analyzed 630 genes in 60 unrelated Utah residents.

Genes sat in high-interest regions, including the ENCODE pilot areas. Of the genes, 374 were expressed in the test cells. Many regions showed significant links between single variants and expression levels. Three correction methods were applied to guard against false hits. Stranger proves expression itself can be mapped like a trait. The genes sat on chromosome 21, chromosome 20, and in ENCODE zones.
europmc-pmc1413581:
Could eating blueberries slow aging? Wilson and co-authors tested that idea in 2006 using a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, a common lab stand-in for aging work. They fed worms a mix of blueberry polyphenols, plant compounds often praised as health aids.

Worms on the mix lived longer and kept moving better as they aged. The mix also helped worms survive heat stress, but not a chemical stress test. Wilson split the mix into three parts. Only the part rich in one compound class gave the gain. The effect needed a gene pathway tied to salt stress defense, not the usual stress routes.
europmc-pmc1552081:
Reviews of test accuracy studies had no software of their own. Zamora and co-authors built one in 2006, called Meta-DiSc. Such reviews pool studies of how well a medical test spots disease. Analysts had to borrow general stats tools.

Meta-DiSc checks why results differ between studies and pools sensitivity and specificity, the two core accuracy measures. It handles both fixed and random effects models and draws forest plots and summary curves ready for papers. Its math was checked against other tools and published reviews. Zamora offers the Windows program free for academic use.
europmc-pmc1626481:
Meta-analysis software can be pricey and hard to learn. Bax and co-authors built a free alternative in 2006, called MIX. It pools results across studies to judge therapies and disease causes. Their target users were students and researchers new to the method.

MIX runs inside Excel, using its sheets for calculation and Visual Basic for the interface. Built-in tutoring tools guide users, and the design pairs with standard textbooks. To validate it, Bax re-ran eight published meta-analyses and matched outputs against two reference programs, STATA and Comprehensive Meta-Analysis. The results agreed, supporting MIX as a teaching-friendly tool.
europmc-pmc1634881:
Oceans swarm with viruses, most of them unknown to science. Angly and co-authors surveyed them in 2006 across four ocean regions, from 184 viral samples at 68 sites gathered over a decade.

Most sequences matched nothing in current databases. Global diversity ran to several hundred thousand species by their estimate. Richness varied with latitude, richer toward the south in their gradient. The Sargasso Sea teemed with cyanophages, while Arctic samples held many prophage-like sequences. Yet most species appeared in many regions. Angly concludes local conditions enrich common types rather than excluding others outright.
europmc-pmc2062481: Impact of artemisinin-based combination therapy and insecticide-treated nets on malaria burden in Zanzibar. — a 2005 science paper on malaria control in Zanzibar. It measures the malaria burden. The paper is the malaria-control study: the findings on Zanzibar, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2292181: Identification of novel and candidate miRNAs in rice by high throughput sequencing. — a 2005 science paper on rice miRNA discovery. It identifies the novel miRNAs. The paper is the discovery study: the findings on rice, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2361981: NK105, a paclitaxel-incorporating micellar nanoparticle formulation, can extend in vivo antitum — a 2008 science paper on the NK105 drug. It extends the antitumor effect. The paper is the NK105 study: the findings on the drug, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2365981: Mapping the genetic architecture of gene expression in human liver. — a 2008 science paper on liver gene architecture. It maps the genetic architecture. The paper is the mapping study: the findings on liver, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2492881: A comprehensive comparison of random forests and support vector machines for microarray-based c — a 2008 science paper on forests vs SVMs. It compares the classifiers. The paper is the compare study: the findings on microarray ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2515281: Multiparameter flow cytometric analysis of CD4 and CD8 T cell subsets in young and old people. — a 2008 science paper on T-cell subset counts. It analyzes the CD4/CD8 subsets. The paper is the count study: the findings on T cells, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2516581: Estimating community drug abuse by wastewater analysis. — a 2008 science paper on wastewater drug surveys. It estimates the drug abuse for labs. The paper is the estimate study: the findings on drugs, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2605581: Review on solving the inverse problem in EEG source analysis. — a 2008 science paper on the EEG inverse problem. It reviews the inverse solving. The paper is the review study: the findings on EEG ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2642881: Causal modelling and brain connectivity in functional magnetic resonance imaging. — a 2008 science paper on causal brain modeling. It models the causal connectivity. The paper is the model study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2718581: Schizophrenia and violence: systematic review and meta-analysis. — a 2008 science paper on schizophrenia. It reviews the systematic evidence. The paper is the violence review: the findings on schizophrenia ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily.
europmc-pmc2719581: Hippocampal atrophy as a quantitative trait in a genome-wide association study identifying nove — a 2008 science paper on hippocampal atrophy. It identifies the novel trait genes. The paper is the trait study: the findings on hippocampus ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2746281: Masitinib (AB1010), a potent and selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting KIT. — a 2008 science paper on a KIT-blocking pill. It blocks the KIT for labs. The paper is the pill study: the notes on pill ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2771281: HIV/AIDS among inmates of and releasees from US correctional facilities, 2006: declining share — a 2008 science paper on HIV in correctional facilities. It tracks the declining share. The paper is the tracking study: the findings on inmate ills, filed here in session.
mesmer-precis-historique-1781:
Mesmer published his Précis historique in 1781 to set out the facts of animal magnetism as he saw them. The pamphlet is his own historical summary, written before the royal commissions of 1784 condemned his claims. It is a pivotal firsthand source for the birth of mesmerism.

Mesmer recounts his early cures and the resistance of the medical world. He presents case after case as proof of his unseen fluid. Rivals, jealous doctors, and blind prejudice explain, in his telling, every failure to win acceptance. The founder tells his story here in full, on his own terms. Later histories of the affair all lean on this defense.
anania-de-natura-daemonum-latin-1581:
Gian Lorenzo Anania, an Italian priest, published De natura daemonum in 1581. The Latin work runs to four books on the nature, orders, and operations of demons. It belongs to the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic answer to Protestant reform, and it sums up demon lore in scholastic order.

Anania sorts demons by rank and task, as a naturalist sorts beasts. He explains how they act on bodies, minds, and the weather. Scripture and the church fathers supply his evidence throughout. The tone is calm, learned, and certain. Readers meet demons catalogued like specimens, in the most orderly demonology of its Italian moment.
bodin-de-magorum-daemonomania-latin-1581:
Bodin's Démonomanie reached learned Europe in this Latin translation, printed at Basel in 1581. The translator worked under the pen name Lotarius Philoponus. Latin carried Bodin's legal demonology to judges and scholars who read no French, greatly widening the book's power.

The four books define sorcery, weigh evidence, and prescribe punishments with a lawyer's care. Bodin's rigor answered Weyer's doubts and hardened witchcraft theory into law. This complete Latin text spread that theory far beyond France. It belongs beside the French original of 1580 in any serious study. Together they show how one jurist's book could steer trials across a continent.
jacquier-flagellum-haereticorum-latin-15:
Nicolas Jacquier, a Dominican inquisitor, wrote his Flagellum haereticorum fascinariorum, the Scourge of Heretical Witches, in 1458. This text comes from the edition of 1581, which kept his argument in circulation. Jacquier's target is the old Canon Episcopi, whose skepticism about night flights he sets out to demolish.

He insists that witches truly gather, body and soul, at their assemblies. That claim made the sabbath real for learned theology. Scholars call his book the pivot of fifteenth-century demonology. After Jacquier, doubt needed defending and belief needed only citing. The Latin scourge turned learned opinion toward the burning dogma that shaped the great hunts.
plos-pone-0004881:
Chao Zhang and colleagues reported S9, a novel anticancer agent interfering with PI3K Akt mTOR signaling and microtubules, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Deregulation of the PI3K Akt mTOR pathway plays central roles in tumor formation and progression, providing validated therapy targets. S9, a hybrid of lactone and indole compounds, exerts anti proliferative activity by simultaneously disrupting signaling and the microtubule cytoskeleton in cancer cell models.

Dual action may delay resistance emergence. Hybrid design merges two pharmacophores productively. Cell division and growth signals fall together. Further growth requires animal testing. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004981:
Protein domains are the building blocks of proteins. Members of one superfamily share a core shape. Yet their lengths can differ greatly. Sankaran Sandhya and colleagues studied those differences in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on superfamilies with large length variation. The variation exceeded thirty percent in the cases they examined.

Extra or missing pieces are called indels. The study asked how indels in a domain scaffold change structure and function. Some length changes matter greatly. Others are absorbed by the core without harm. The survey is a field guide to protein remodeling. It helps predict which changes a protein can tolerate.
plos-pone-0005081:
Male-pattern baldness is tied to the androgen receptor gene. The exact DNA change behind the link was unidentified. Joanna Cobb and colleagues tested one candidate in PLOS ONE in 2009. The candidate was copy number variation. Such variation duplicates or deletes large DNA segments. They ran a case-control study on androgenetic alopecia.

The study asked whether receptor copy changes explain the association. Their results probe that hypothesis directly. Even a negative answer narrows the hunt. The functional variant must lie elsewhere in or near the gene. Baldness genetics is a model for common trait genetics. Each excluded suspect sharpens the search. The work keeps that search honest.
plos-pone-0005181:
An enzyme called heparanase cuts through the mesh that surrounds cells. Most human cancers make too much of it, which helps tumors spread and grow new blood vessels. Zcharia and colleagues built mice with the heparanase gene removed and reported the results in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The new mice showed that heparanase and a second family of cutting enzymes, the matrix metalloproteinases, are controlled together. When one is gone, the other shifts as well. That linked control matters for drug design, since blocking one enzyme alone may not stop tumors from cutting their way out.
plos-pone-0005281:
Histoplasma capsulatum is a fungus that causes lung disease, and it secretes an enzyme activity called DppIV. Cooper and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the fungus has two genes for that enzyme family, and one does most of the secreted work.

The enzyme can cut substance P, a human peptide that helps regulate immune responses. Cutting a host signal peptide could blunt the body's alarm against the fungus. The finding names a possible immune-evasion trick and a fungal enzyme that drugs might target. A germ that cuts a host alarm wire must first make the tool and send it out,. Each of those steps is a place where a new drug might jam its work.
plos-pone-0005881:
Sarah Devantier and co-authors watched in 2009 how doctors sort patients when forced to choose which of two a third most resembles. Experts in many fields see the deep structure of a problem where novices see surface details. Whether that holds in clinical reasoning was less studied.

In the triad task, clinicians grouped patients, revealing how context shapes their categories. Their choices integrated background information into management thinking, not just symptoms. Understanding that integration helps train doctors and design decision aids. The study treats diagnosis as thinking, not mere pattern matching, and shows the context experts silently include.
plos-pone-0005981:
Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body itself. Timothy Radstake, Lenny van Bon, Jasper Broen and colleagues asked whether those peacekeepers fail in systemic sclerosis, a disease that hardens skin and organs. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study compares patients with limited and with diffuse forms of the disease.

Patients had more regulatory cells, not fewer, but the cells worked less well. The flaw tracked with low levels of CD69 and of TGF-beta, two signs of a working peacekeeper. A larger but weaker guard force fits a disease of slow self-attack, and the named markers give clinics a way to gauge the failure.
plos-pone-0006081:
How a molecule leaves its pocket in a protein is as telling as how it enters. Dong Long, Yuguang Mu and Daiwen Yang simulated that exit in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper models ligand dissociation from liver fatty acid binding protein, a carrier that holds fatty acids and, unusually, can fit two molecules in its cavity at once.

Entry and exit routes for this protein family had puzzled the field for decades. A simulation can watch the exit frame by frame, which no bench test can do. The route it finds helps explain how the carrier loads and unloads its cargo, a basic step in how the liver handles fat and some drugs.
plos-pone-0006181:
Cells pause and repair themselves when their DNA is damaged, rather than dividing with broken instructions. Domenica Paparatto and colleagues studied two guard kinases, Chk1 and Cds1, in fission yeast for a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They exposed the yeast to cisplatin, a cancer drug that harms DNA, and watched how the guards affected survival.

Both kinases proved important for yeast cells to live through the drug's damage. The guards delay division, buying time for repair work to finish. Yeast is a simple stand-in for the same safety system in human cells. Understanding it helps explain why some cancer cells resist drugs that attack DNA.
plos-pone-0006681:
Dena L. Schanzer and colleagues modeled influenza testing in Canada for PLOS ONE in 2009. Public health systems watch the weekly share of lab tests positive for influenza. That share helps officials spot periods of flu activity. How well it works depends on the sensitivity of the testing itself. A test that misses cases can distort the picture of a season.

The team used modelling to estimate that sensitivity from national data. They drew on results from a national respiratory virus detection program. Their estimates show how much influenza laboratory testing likely catches or misses. Knowing the limits of the test helps interpret surveillance numbers honestly. It can also guide improvements in how Canada tracks flu each year.
plos-pone-0006781:
Christian Rabeling and his team found an ant whose queens need no mates in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sex rules in most of life, though it costs more than cloning. Mixing genes speeds change and clears bad gene faults. True cases of sex-free life are rare and prized as proof. The ant is Mycocepurus smithii, which farms fungus for food.

The team showed this ant breeds by thelytokous parthenogenesis. In plain words, females hatch from eggs no male has touched. Queens can fill a nest with daughters on their own. An ant that skips sex breaks the rules for social insects. It helps science weigh what sex is truly worth.
plos-pone-0006881:
Yuki Kawakubo and his team gauged blood flow in the front brain of youths with autism in PLOS ONE in 2009. Faults in that brain zone have long been tied to autism. Close kin of those with autism can show odd brain acts too. Tests of social skill bring some of those gaps to light. How the front brain grows up was less clear.

Growth of the front brain's blood flow lagged in autism. Kin with no autism shared part of that lag. A trait found in kin may mark a passed-down weak point. Blood flow tests are pain-free and safe for youths. The mark could help track growth and test early help.
plos-pone-0006981:
Pankaj Goyal, Antje Behring, Abhishek Kumar, and colleagues described a little-known enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human kinome holds hundreds of protein kinases. More than a hundred of them had unknown jobs at the time. One was STK35, a serine-threonine kinase in a small kinase family.

The team identified and characterized a form named STK35L1. They also traced its counterparts and close relatives across vertebrates. Mapping a kinase's family tree is the first step to finding what it switches on. Any of these unstudied kinases could later prove to be a drug target.
plos-pone-0007081: David Metzgar, Greg Skochko, Carl Gibbins, and colleagues evaluated and validated a real-time PCR test for human adenovirus 14 in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their assay was built to detect the virus in patient samples and to count how much was present. A validated test of this kind gives clinics and labs a trusted way to spot this adenovirus strain during outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007181:
Derek M. Dykxhoorn, Yichao Wu, Huangming Xie, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on breast cancer spread. Cancer becomes most dangerous when cells leave the first tumor and colonize distant tissues. That last step, forming new tumors far away, is the least understood part of metastasis.

The authors study a small RNA molecule called miR-200 in mouse breast cancer cells. They report that miR-200 helps cancer cells colonize distant sites and form metastases. Their work points to colonization, not just invasion, as a step worth targeting in treatment research.
plos-pone-0007281:
Christopher R. Cederroth and Serge Nef studied early diet and adult sugar control in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Dietary soy and its phytoestrogens may benefit fat and glucose metabolism. The authors had shown that males fed high soy from conception had lower weight and fat as adults.

The authors now examine fetal programming of adult glucose homeostasis. They ask how early soy exposure sets later blood sugar regulation. Their mouse work tests whether effects begin before birth rather than only through adult diet. The findings inform debates about soy feeding in early life.
openalex-w2099735981: South America's seas stretch 30,000 km — knowledge is patchy. Miloslavich and colleagues' 2011 review surveyed marine biodiversity on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of South America. The work mapped knowledge and gaps across three domains.
openalex-w2116492181: The brain's border is run by star-shaped cells. A 2014 review covers astrocyte modulation of the blood-brain barrier, with perspectives on Parkinson's disease. The review weighed how astrocytes could become drug targets — glia as medicine, reviewed in depth.
plos-pone-0006281:
Plague bacteria carry a versatile weapon called the V antigen on a small extra DNA ring. Tracy DiMezzo and colleagues tracked that antigen inside infected cells grown in the lab, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. V can quiet the host immune response and also helps switch on other attack proteins.

The team followed where V travels within cells during Yersinia pestis infection. Its route and timing were largely unmapped before this work. A clear trafficking map fills a gap in how plague disarms its host. The details may expose points where the process can be blocked.
openalex-w2195279081: In much of the world, people die without a doctor certifying the cause — so health officials interview families instead, in "verbal autopsies." This 2015 BMC Medicine paper improves the Tariff Method, an algorithm that assigns causes of death from those interviews. More accurate cause-of-death data means better public-health decisions in places where death certificates are rare.
openalex-w2252702481: Helium nuclei raining down from space carry clues about where cosmic rays are born and how they travel. This 2015 Physical Review Letters paper reports a precision measurement of the helium flux — from 1.9 GV to 3 TV in rigidity — by the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer aboard the International Space Station, based on 50 million events. The exact shape of that spectrum constrains theories of cosmic-ray origin and acceleration.
openalex-w2290369781: Breeders have genotyping for genes and phenotyping for traits — now comes a third 'typing' for the environment itself. This 2016 paper proposes 'envirotyping': systematically measuring the environmental conditions crops face, to decipher how climate change impacts production. Combined with genetic and trait data, it promises a fuller picture of why crops thrive or fail in a shifting climate.
openalex-w264334781: The lung cavities of tuberculosis — which spread the bacillus — form when lung matrix is destroyed, but how was unclear. This 2015 PLoS Pathogens paper fingers neutrophil-derived MMP-8, showing it drives AMPK-dependent matrix destruction in human pulmonary TB. The mechanism spotlights the immune system's own enzymes as the wrecking crew — and a potential therapeutic target.
openalex-w2773939681: Metagenomics software promises to identify microbes from DNA soup — but which tools actually work? This 2017 Nature Methods paper reports the Critical Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation (CAMI), a benchmark of assembly, taxonomic profiling, and binning methods. The standardized contest exposes strengths and weaknesses across the field's key algorithms.
openalex-w2782327081: Zika's cruelest legacy was microcephaly — babies born with shrunken brains. This 2018 Scientific Reports study examines the immune response and cell-damage mechanisms in the central nervous systems of fatal microcephaly cases. The in situ analysis traces how the virus ravages the developing brain, defining what is now called congenital Zika syndrome.
openalex-w2809684781: Machine learning is surging into computer networks — but the literature is scattered. This 2018 Journal of Internet Services and Applications paper surveys ML for networking comprehensively: its evolution, applications, and open research opportunities. The review maps where learning algorithms are reshaping how networks run.
openalex-w4414770781: This 2025 Lancet paper — by Willett, Rockström, Springmann and colleagues — presents the EAT-Lancet Commission on healthy, sustainable, and just food systems. The landmark report charts how to feed humanity within planetary boundaries.
europmc-pmc2850381: Before a cell divides, its nucleus and centrosome must move into position. This 2010 paper shows the motor proteins dynein and kinesin-1, linked by Bicaudal D2, associate with nuclear pores to regulate that positioning during mitotic entry. The authors map the machinery. Their work reveals the logistics behind cell division.
europmc-pmc2870981: A century-old chemical reaction keeps finding new tricks. This 2010 review tours new developments in the Friedel-Crafts alkylation, from green chemistry to asymmetric catalysis. The authors show an old workhorse renewed. Their tour connects classic organic chemistry to modern clean methods.
europmc-pmc2872881: Pea aphids live with many microbes yet rarely get sick, and this 2010 paper asks why. The authors survey immunity and other defenses in the pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum. Their overview reveals unusual immune gaps. The work explains how a major crop pest tolerates its germ load.
